viparyasto bhavedyatra vyutkramaṃ tannigadyate // Ckc_2.10 //
children.translated_text: Where the proper sequence of the word or meaning to be employed is reversed, that is called <s>vyutkrama</s> (disordered sequence). [Ckc 2.10]
For example:
O <s>Śrī Siṅgabhūpāla</s>! In prowess and might, you are like <s>Bhīma</s>; as <s>Darpaka</s> (Cupid) and slayer of <s>Kīcaka</s>,

children.text: ādeśanivahividhau gurūṇāṃ yathā rāghavabhārgavau tvam // Ckc_2.*10 //
children.translated_text: in the manner of dispensing commands to the preceptors, you are like <s>Rāghava</s> and <s>Bhārgava</s>. [Ckc 2.10*]

children.text:
atra bale prabhāve ceti sāmānyadharmaparigaṇanākramavaśādupamānayorapi taddharmiṇoḥ krameṇoktireva yukteti kīcakadarpakārīti vaktavye vyutkameṇa bhaṇanācchabdavyutkamamidam /
atraiva rāghavādapi bhārgavasyābhyarhitatvād bhārgavarāghavāviti vaktavye tadatikramya nirdeśādarthavyutkramamidama /
ubhayatrāpi kīcakadarpakārī bhārgavarāghavāviti ca pāṭho ramaṇīyaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, since the order of enumerating the common attributes (<s>sāmānyadharma</s>) — 'in strength' and 'in might' — requires mentioning the corresponding exemplars in the same order, one should have said '<s>Kīcaka-Darpakārī</s>' [instead of '<s>Darpaka-Kīcakārī</s>'] — thus this is a <s>śabdavyutkrama</s> (verbal disorder). Furthermore, since <s>Bhārgava</s> (<s>Paraśurāma</s>) is more venerable than <s>Rāghava</s> (<s>Rāma</s>), one should have said '<s>Bhārgava-Rāghavau</s>' — the transgression of this order constitutes <s>arthavyutkrama</s> (semantic disorder). In both cases, the readings '<s>Kīcaka-Darpakārī</s>' and '<s>Bhārgava-Rāghavau</s>' are preferable.
When there is no intended distinction [in ordering], when doubt is to be dispelled,
and when brevity of expression is facilitated — even this [disordered sequence] is to be honored [as a merit]. [Ckc 2.11]
An example in the case of no intended distinction:

children.text: ghaṭāmaḥ svīyaṃ vā puratatimanarghyānapi maṇī-nakharvāmuvīṃ vāvisṛja gatiranyā na mahatā /
children.translated_text: Let us build our own fortress, or release the priceless jewels, or set free the vast earth — there is no other recourse for the great.

children.text: tvayā grāhyaṃ siṅgakṣitibhuji na vairaṃ priyatam priyāṇāmasmākaṃ vacanamucitaṃ māsma paribhūḥ // Ckc_2.*11 //
children.translated_text: O King <s>Siṅga</s>, ruler of the earth! You should accept [this] — not enmity. This is the fitting counsel of us who are your well-wishers; do not disregard it! [Ckc 2.11*]

children.text:
atra puradeśagajāśvaratnānāmabhyarhitatvāt pūrvapūrvaṃ nirdeśaḥ /
athavā na visarjanakriyāsambandhādanabhyarhitānāṃ pūrvapūrvamuddeśaḥ kartavyaḥ /
evaṃ satyuktaprakāreṇātikrame 'pi prāṇeśvara sakalamapi dhanaṃ svāmine samarpya prāṇā rakṣaṇīyāḥ /
kṛtamabhyahitānabhyarhitavivekeneti vivakṣayā śatrukāntābhirūktatvād duṣṭatvam /

children.translated_text: An example of removing doubt, in the genealogy of the hero himself:

children.text: yasyādyo viditaḥ kumāratilakaḥ śrīyannavoto guṇairekasyāgrajamātmarūpavibhave cāpe dvayoragrajam /
children.translated_text: He whose first [ancestor] is known as the crest-jewel of princes, <s>Śrī Yannavota</s>, in virtues surpassing the elder brother of one; in his own splendor and power, surpassing the elder brothers of two;

children.text: ārūḍhe tritayāgrajaṃ vijayate durvāradorvikrame satyoktau caturagrajaṃ vitaraṇe kiñcāpi pañcāgrajam // Ckc_2.*12 //
children.translated_text: having ascended, with irresistible arm-prowess, he surpasses the elder brother of three; in truthful speech, the elder brother of four; and in generosity, even the elder brother of five. [Ckc 2.12*]

Here, since forts, territories, elephants, horses, and jewels are [listed] in order of venerability, the first should be mentioned first. Alternatively, since they are connected with the act of relinquishing, the less venerable should be mentioned first. Given this, even though there is a transgression of the stated order, the [speakers being] enemy wives [say]: 'O lord of our lives, having surrendered all wealth to the master, our lives should be saved — enough with the distinction between venerable and non-venerable!' — with this intention, and because it is spoken by the enemy's wives, there is a fault.

children.text: atra karṇādīnāmabhyarhitatvāt pañcānāmagrajaṃ trayāṇāmagrajaṃ dvayohagrajamekasyāgrajamiti vaktavye 'pi saṃkhyāpacayasūcitāpraśastipratītiparihārāya saṃkhyopacayatvāropeṇo ttarottarābhivṛddhidyotanādapakrape 'pi kramādatisundara iti guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, since <s>Karṇa</s> and others are more venerable, one should have said 'elder brother of five, elder brother of three, elder brother of two, elder brother of one' — but to avoid the impression of decreasing prestige suggested by decreasing numbers, by imposing an ascending numerical sequence to indicate successive increasing eminence, even with the disordered sequence, it is extremely beautiful — hence it is a merit.
An example in the case of facilitating brevity of expression:
O <s>Śrī Siṅgabhūpāla</s>! The <s>Rāmas</s> are four, clearly portions of <s>Hari</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>).

children.text: samau tatra mahodāttau viṣamau tu mahoddhatau // Ckc_2.*13 //
children.translated_text: Among them, two are equal — the magnanimous and the exalted; and two are unequal — the mighty and the impetuous. [Ckc 2.13*]

children.text:
atra kṛtatretādvāparakaliyugeṣu bhārgavo rāghavo yādava iti trayo rāmāḥ śrīsiṅgabhūpālaśceti catvāro lokarakṣāpekṣayā śrīviṣṇoraṃśā ityuktāḥ /
teṣu caturṣu prathama uddhato dvitīya udāttaḥ tṛtīyaścoddhataśvaturtha udātta iti vaktavye paṭhitaprakāreṇa vyutkrame 'pi samāviti dvitīyacaturthayordaśarathānnavotasaṃbhūtayo raṃśayoḥ, viṣamāviti reṇukārohiṇīgarbhasaṃbhūtayoḥ prathamatṛtīyayoraṃśayośva dhīrodāttadhīroddhatatvaguṇasāmyasaṃbandhānusandhāyinā saṃkṣopoktisaukarye 'pi cārutā samunmīlatīti guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Here it is stated that the four <s>Rāmas</s> — <s>Bhārgava</s> (<s>Paraśurāma</s>) in <s>Kṛtayuga</s>, <s>Rāghava</s> (<s>Rāma</s>) in <s>Tretāyuga</s>, <s>Yādava</s> (<s>Balarāma</s>) in <s>Dvāparayuga</s>, and <s>Śrī Siṅgabhūpāla</s> in <s>Kaliyuga</s> — are portions of <s>Śrī Viṣṇu</s> for the protection of the world. Among these four, where one should say 'the first is impetuous (<s>uddhata</s>), the second is exalted (<s>udātta</s>), the third also impetuous, and the fourth also exalted,' the stated form with '<s>samau</s>' (equal pair) for the second and fourth — the portions born of <s>Daśaratha</s> and <s>Yannavota</s> — and '<s>viṣamau</s>' (unequal pair) for the first and third — the portions born from <s>Reṇukā</s> and <s>Rohiṇī</s> — achieves beauty even with the disordered sequence, because one perceives the connection of similarity in the <s>dhīrodātta</s> (calm-exalted) and <s>dhīroddhata</s> (calm-impetuous) hero-types through the facilitation of concise expression. Hence it is a merit.
<s>Punarukti</s> (redundancy) is where a word [is repeated] that is not different from [another word's] meaning. [Ckc 2.12]
O <s>Siṅghanṛpāla</s> (King <s>Siṅgha</s>)! Worthy of service by the elephant-riders and the faithful, O terror of the wicked!
The thunder and pomp of your threats remains — the arrogance of <s>Śambara</s> is shed like the ichor of a maddened elephant. [Ckc 2.14*]
Here, since '<s>ḍambara</s>' appears in identical form [in both '<s>garjita-ḍambara</s>' and '<s>Śambara-ḍambara</s>'], there is verbal redundancy (<s>padapunarukti</s>).
Even this [fault] is to be honored when the intention is to express the intensification of emotion (<s>bhāvotkarṣa</s>). [Ckc 2.13]

children.text: yathā dayodadhe tvaṃ naḥ pāhi pāhi naḥ karuṇāṃbudhe /
children.translated_text: As follows: "O ocean of compassion, protect us, protect us, O cloud of mercy!

children.text: poṣyā vayaṃ na vidveṣyāḥ siṅgabhūpāla pālaya // Ckc_2.*15 //
children.translated_text: We are to be nourished, not despised — O King <s>Siṅgabhūpāla</s>, protect us!" // Ckc_2.*15 //

children.text:
atra karuṇāṃbudhe dayodadhe ityarthapunaruktiḥ /
pāhi naḥ pāhi na iti śabdapunaruktiḥ /
tadubhayamapi śatṛsaṃbandhikā vigrahakārigatadainyātiśayavivakṣāyāṃ na duṣyati kintu svārthātiśayaṃ puṣyatīti guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, 'O cloud of mercy' and 'O ocean of compassion' constitute a repetition of meaning (<s>arthapunarukti</s>). 'Protect us, protect us' constitutes a repetition of words (<s>śabdapunarukti</s>). Both of these, in the context of expressing the intensity of the supplicant's distress related to the oppressor's hostility, are not faulty but rather enhance the intended sense — hence they constitute a merit (<s>guṇa</s>).
Where there is a conjunction of words that are naturally distant in construal — that is called <s>duranvaya</s> (difficult construal). // Ckc_2.14 //
As follows:

children.text: śrīsiṅgakṣitipālasaṅgarataleṣvaṅgāni dṛṣṭvā dviṣāmātaṅkena samantataḥ kilakilārāveṇa vaitālikāḥ /
children.translated_text: On the battlefields of King <s>Siṅga</s>, seeing the limbs of enemies, the <s>vaitālikas</s> (bards) cry out in terror with shrill <s>kilakilā</s> cries all around;

children.text: kāntāḥ khaṇḍavikhṇḍatāṃ parigatānyuccaṇḍakhaḍgāhateḥ ghorāḥ kaṅkakulākuleṣu cakitāśvinvanti minvanti ca // Ckc_2.*16 //
children.translated_text: the beloved (limbs), having been hacked to pieces by the fierce sword-blows, amid the tumult of vulture-flocks — terrified, they tremble and quake. // Ckc_2.*16 //

children.text:
atra kaṅkakulākuleṣu saṅgareṣvityanayorātaṅkena cakitā ityanayoḥ kilakilārāveṇa ghorā ityanayorvaitālikā duṣṭvetyanayoratipratyāsattikāṅkṣiṇoḥ dūradūrā vighaṭanā dṛśyate /
seyamanvayāvasare sarasamānasaṃ duḥkhākarotīti duranvayaṃ duṣṭam /
children.translated_text: Here, between 'amid the vulture-flocks' and 'on the battlefields,' between 'in terror' and 'terrified,' between 'with shrill cries' and 'fierce,' and between 'bards' and 'wicked' — (words) that require close proximity in construal are separated far apart. This (verse), when construed, causes great distress to the connoisseur's mind — hence the <s>duranvaya</s> is a fault (<s>duṣṭa</s>).
Sometimes even this (duranvaya) is found to have the status of a merit (<s>guṇa</s>). // Ckc_2.15 //
As follows:
Some milkers made themselves protectors of the cows as cowherds (<s>gopāla</s>);

children.text: sā paraṃ siṅgabhūpena caritārthā vasundharā // Ckc_2.*17 //
children.translated_text: but this earth was truly fulfilled only by King <s>Siṅgabhūpa</s>. // Ckc_2.*17 //

children.text: atra pālayāñcakrire iti vaktavye pālayāṃ kecid gopālāśvakrire iti dūrānvaytve 'pi vyavahitamapīcchanti keciditi viśeṣāvyutvādanād guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, though one should say 'pālayāñcakrire,' the expression 'pālayāṃ kecid gopālāśvakrire' with distant construal — even in this <s>duranvaya</s>, since some accept even the separated (construal), and because the particular distinction is well conveyed — it constitutes a merit (<s>guṇa</s>).
The intermingling of one sentence's components with those of another is called <s>vākyāṅgasaṅkīrṇa</s> (sentence-part confusion). // Ckc_2.16 //
As follows:
Bidding farewell to swords, they march out; they draw and brandish (them against) wives;

children.text: divaṃ muñcanti yānti kṣmāṃ siṅgabhūpālavidviṣaḥ // Ckc_2.*18 //
children.translated_text: they abandon heaven, they go to the earth — (such are) the enemies of King <s>Siṅgabhūpāla</s>. // Ckc_2.*18 //

children.text: atra vadhūrāpṛcchya niryānti khaḍgānākṛṣya dhunvate kṣmāṃ muñcanti divaṃ yānti iti vaktavye vākyayoḥ parasparapadasaṅkaraḥ kṛta iti vākyāṅgasaṅikīrṇamidam /
children.translated_text: Here, instead of saying 'bidding farewell to wives, they march out; drawing swords, they brandish them; they abandon the earth, they go to heaven' — the words of the (two) sentences have been intermingled with each other, hence this is <s>vākyāṅgasaṅkīrṇa</s> (sentence-part confusion).

children.text: vākyaṃ vākyādike tacca guṇībhāvena bhāvyate // Ckc_2.17 //
children.translated_text: A sentence (placed) at the beginning of another sentence — that too should be regarded as having the status of a subordinate element. // Ckc_2.17 //
As follows:

children.text: vācāmīśa sureśa daivataguro tvāmapyajaiṣītkila prajñāyāmanavotasiṅganṛpatiḥ sacve tadairāvatam /
children.translated_text: O lord of speech, O lord of gods, O preceptor of the gods — even you were conquered by King <s>Siṅga</s>, that foremost in wisdom; truly, (he conquered even) <s>Airāvata</s> (Indra's elephant);

children.text: dāne kalpatarūn jitā vayamamī tatsāṃprataṃ sāṃprataṃ bhoge svāmini nirjite tvayi yathā rājā tathā hi prajāḥ // Ckc_2.*19 //
children.translated_text: in generosity, the wish-fulfilling trees were surpassed — we are vanquished! Now, now, O master, in enjoyment — when you are conquered, as is the king so are the subjects. // Ckc_2.*19 //

children.text:
atra vācāmīśa daivataguro tvāmapyajaiṣīdityekaṃ vākyam /
sureśa vayaṃ jitā ityapararaṃ prativākyam /
tayoraṃśabhūtasambuddhipadasaṅkare 'pi vākyopavākyatvānna doṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, 'O lord of speech, O preceptor of the gods, even you were conquered' is one sentence. 'O lord of gods, we are vanquished' is another, a counter-sentence. Even though there is intermingling of the vocative words that form parts of these (sentences), since (the intermingled parts function as) sentence and sub-sentence, there is no fault.
<s>Vākyagarbhita</s> (sentence-within-sentence) — that within whose interior another sentence resides. // Ckc_2.18 //
As follows:
Before your sword, O king, which is as cruel as the fangs of <s>Kṛtānta</s> (Death),

children.text: kā hi śaṅkā madāndhānāṃ tiṣṭhanti śatrubhūvarāḥ // Ckc_2.*20 //
children.translated_text: what fear is there? — (yet) the intoxicated enemy kings stand (their ground). // Ckc_2.*20 //

children.text: atra nāyaka tava khaḍgāya śatrubhūpāstiṣṭhantīti vākyasya garbhe kā hi śaṅkā madāndhānāmiti vakyāntaramavikalaṃ sthitamiti tadidaṃ vākthagabhitam /
children.translated_text: Here, within the sentence 'O hero, the enemy kings stand before your sword,' the complete sentence 'what fear is there of the intoxicated ones?' resides intact within it — hence this is <s>vākyagarbhita</s> (sentence-within-sentence).
This (figure) delights connoisseurs when it serves to indicate one's own state and similar (purposes). // Ckc_2.19 //
As follows:

children.text: sakhyaśvandramukho niṣiñca caraṇe mandākine candanaṃ padmākṣaḥ sakhi padmakī madhukarau padmena nirvāpaya /
children.translated_text: "Friend, the moon-faced one — sprinkle sandalwood on (his) feet! O <s>Mandākinī</s>! The lotus-eyed one — dear friend <s>Padmakī</s>, fan away the bees with a lotus!

children.text: smeraśrīr naya śārikāṃ caturikāṃ dūraṃ durālāpinīṃ śrīsiṅge hṛdayaṅgamo mama paraḥ kiṃ jalpitaiḥ kalpitaiḥ // Ckc_2.*21 //
children.translated_text: The one whose beauty smiles — take the <s>śārikā</s> (myna bird) away, and the clever maid who speaks harmful words, far away! O <s>Śrī Siṅga</s>, my heart's beloved — what use are (your) speeches and contrivances?" // Ckc_2.*21 //

children.text:
atra he sakhyaḥ candramukhaḥ padmākṣaḥ smeraśrīḥ nāyako me hṛdayaṅgamo nāyaka iti vākyasya niṣiñca caraṇāvityādinā sakhi padmake mametyādinā naya śārikāmityādinā /
vākyatrayeṇa pratipāditaṃ garbhitatve 'pi nāyikāyāḥ nāyakaguṇa saṅkīrtanakramasamārūḍhasaṃtāpodvegādilakṣaṇakāmāvasthātiśayasūcakatvena sahṛdayahṛdayāhlādanād guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, the sentence 'O friends, the moon-faced, lotus-eyed, beauty-smiling hero is my heart's beloved' — this (main) sentence, through the three subordinate sentences 'sprinkle on the feet' and so on, 'O dear friend Padmakī, (fan away) for me' and so on, and 'take the myna away' and so on — even though they are embedded, by indicating the stages of passion (<s>kāmāvasthā</s>) — the intensity of ardor arising from the progressive glorification of the hero's qualities by the heroine — this delights the connoisseur's heart, hence it is a merit (<s>guṇa</s>).
Where a simile has different gender (between its terms) — that is called <s>bhinnaliṅga</s> (gender-discordant);
and where the number differs — that is <s>bhinnavacana</s> (number-discordant simile). // Ckc_2.20 //
As follows:

children.text: śāstrādeva sitā prajñā haṃsīva viśadaṃ yaśaḥ /
children.translated_text: From learning itself (comes) your white wisdom, like a female swan (<s>haṃsī</s>); and bright fame,

children.text: tava siṅgamahīpāla śaśīva rūcirā tanūḥ // Ckc_2.*22 //
children.translated_text: O King <s>Siṅga</s>, and a radiant person like the moon (<s>śaśī</s>). // Ckc_2.*22 //
Here, the difference in number and gender between the <s>upamāna</s> (standard of comparison) and <s>upameya</s> (thing compared) is evident.
This becomes a merit when it does not cause discomfort to the discerning. // Ckc_2.21 //
As follows:
Even your wisdom perceives subtle meanings, like (your two) eyes;
and your fame, like the army of King <s>Siṅgabhūpa</s>, transgresses all boundaries. // Ckc_2.*23 //

children.text: atra locane iva prajñā ityupamānopameyayorliṅgavacanabhede 'pi sūkṣmārthagrāhiṇīti viśeṣāvacanaśleṣavaicitrya kṛtisāmarthyena sahṛdayānāmudvego na bhavatīti guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, even though there is a difference in gender and number between the <s>upamāna</s> 'like the eyes' and <s>upameya</s> 'wisdom,' through the skillful artistry of the <s>śleṣa</s> (pun) in the qualifying expression 'perceiver of subtle meanings,' the connoisseur experiences no discomfort — hence it is a merit (<s>guṇa</s>).
Where deficiency or excess in the qualifiers of the standard of comparison

children.text: lakṣyete te krameṇaiva jñeye nyūnādhikopame // Ckc_2.22 //
children.translated_text: is perceived — these are known respectively as <s>nyūnopamā</s> (deficient simile) and <s>adhikopamā</s> (excessive simile). // Ckc_2.22 //
An example of deficient simile (<s>nyūnopamā</s>) —
The head of King <s>Siṅga</s> shines with a canopy (that has) a golden finial,
like the lofty peak of the eastern mountain (<s>Udayādri</s>) with the full-orbed moon. // Ckc_2.*24 //
Here, since some quality of the golden finial (the <s>upamāna</s>) is attributed to the moon as its qualifier, this is a deficient simile (<s>nyūnopama</s>).
An example of excessive simile (<s>adhikopamā</s>) —
King <s>Siṅgabhūpa</s> sits resplendent on the throne, with a shimmering pearl necklace on his chest,
like a wish-fulfilling tree (<s>kalpavṛkṣa</s>) on the slope of Mount <s>Sumeru</s>, radiant with fresh coral clusters in long garlands. // Ckc_2.*25 //
Here, the ruby-qualities of the <s>upameya</s> (the hero) being unstated, while the fresh coral of the <s>upamāna</s> has an excess — this constitutes an excessive simile (<s>adhikopamā</s>).
The wise recognize the merit of both (deficient and excessive similes) through well-known convention and inference. // Ckc_2.23 //
An example of deficient simile becoming a merit —
With a sword-blade that is terrible (and) upraised, trembling like a serpent,
King <s>Siṅgabhūpāla</s> shines like <s>Bhadraśrī</s> (the auspicious elephant) with its trunk. // Ckc_2.*26 //

children.text: atra karavālopamānasya kṛṣṇāheranupādānān nyūnopamatve 'pi vasanti candane kṛṣṇasarpā iti rūḍheranatikleśena tatpratītiriti na duṣṭatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, even though the <s>upamāna</s> of the sword omits mention of the black serpent — making it a deficient simile — since the well-known saying 'black serpents dwell in sandalwood trees' enables recognition without great difficulty, it is not faulty.
An example of the (merit of) excessive simile —
Adorned with necklaces and resplendent in fine garments, the courtesans captivate the mind of the king,

children.text: jyotsnāvisāraviśadā vikacotpalābhā rākāniśā iva virājitalolatārāḥ // Ckc_2.*27 //
children.translated_text: like a full-moon night — radiant with the spread of moonlight, having the appearance of blooming blue lotuses, adorned with glittering stars. // Ckc_2.*27 //

children.text: atra nīlotpalagrahaṇādadhikopamatve 'pi vāravilāsinīkaṭākṣavikṣepayoravinābhāvavijñānapariṇatāntaḥkaraṇānāmupamāno ddhāṭanānumānādanati prayāsena kuvalayopameyānāṃ kaṭākṣavikṣepāṇāṃ pratītiriti guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, even though the mention of blue lotuses creates an excessive simile, for connoisseurs whose minds are well-trained in recognizing the inseparability of the glances of courtesans from their sidelong looks, the <s>upameya</s> of the sidelong glances is easily inferred from the <s>upamāna</s> of blue lotuses — hence it is a merit (<s>guṇa</s>).
Deficiency in meter, caesura (<s>yati</s>), verb, or the like — that is known as <s>vikala</s> (defective). // Ckc_2.24 //
Of these, defective in meter (<s>chandovikala</s>) — as follows:
May <s>Maheśvara</s> (Śiva), whose left side is graced with the beauty of unaffected loveliness, protect
King <s>Siṅgabhūpāla</s>, the crown-jewel of those learned in the arts. // Ckc_2.*28 //
Here, since the third syllable is defective, this is metrically defective (<s>chandovikala</s>).
Elsewhere, even a slight (metrical irregularity) when composed in Prakrit is counted as a merit. // Ckc_2.25 //
As follows:
Of King <s>Siṅgabhūmi</s>, in the middle of the flood-stream of the <s>Gaṅgā</s> of his fame and splendor,

children.text: pariṇhauṇa samaddhaṃ tellokkaṃ hoi parisuddham // Ckc_2.*29 //
children.translated_text: having bathed and been purified, the three worlds become cleansed. // Ckc_2.*29 //

children.text: atra tṛtīyapāde dvitīyavarṇasya saṃyogapūrvatvādgurutvena chandovaikalye 'pi prākṛtādiṣu saṃyuktavarṇānāṃ hvāṇvākāralpakāradīnāṃ tīvraprayatnoccāraṇena pūrvalaghutvaṃ kaiścidiṣṭamiti guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, even though in the third quarter the second syllable being preceded by a conjunct consonant creates a metrical deficiency by being heavy, in Prakrit and similar (languages), since some hold that conjunct consonants and vowels like 'hvā,' 'ṇvā,' 'kā,' 'ra,' 'lpa,' and 'kā' are pronounced with intense effort, the preceding syllable remains light — hence it is a merit (<s>guṇa</s>).
An example of caesura-defective (<s>yativikala</s>) —

children.text: nityaṃ toyadhimaṇimekhalāṃ dharitrīṃ śrīsiṅgakṣitibhujī rakṣitaṃ pravṛtte /
children.translated_text: While King <s>Siṅga</s>, the sovereign of the earth, continually protects the earth wearing the girdle of cloud-jewels,

children.text: vidveṣṭān bhajati vanipatāvanīpān mitrāṇi sphuṭamavanipatāvanīpāt // Ckc_2.*30 //
children.translated_text: the enemies resort to forest-trees for shelter, (while) allies clearly (resort to) forest-trees (for shade from the sun). // Ckc_2.*30 //

children.text: atra tṛtīyasthāne yatau kartavyāyāṃ prathamapāde tathā na kṛtamiti yativikalamidam /
children.translated_text: Here, in the first quarter, the caesura (<s>yati</s>) that should occur at the third position has not been observed — hence this is caesura-defective (<s>yativikala</s>).
This is considered to become a merit through the effect of vowel <s>sandhi</s> (euphonic combination). // Ckc_2.26 //
As follows:

children.text: śrīsiṅgakṣitipāla tāvakacamūdhāṭībhayāṭīkitānākārairapi śābarairapi hitān ghorāṅgame phakkaṇe /
children.translated_text: O King <s>Siṅga</s>, (even) the <s>Śabara</s> tribesmen marked by the terrified gestures of those fleeing in fear from the onslaught of your army,

children.text: ātmīyaiva hi paśyatāṃ piśunayatyābālagopālakaṃ bhūpālān kuliśātapatrakaraśīcihnā padānāṃ tatiḥ // Ckc_2.*31 //
children.translated_text: and the <s>Phakkaṇa</s> (frontier people) with their fierce bodies — your own row of footprints bearing the marks of thunderbolt, parasol, and hand exposes them, from child to cowherd, to be (nothing but) kings. // Ckc_2.*31 //

children.text: atra dvādaśasthāne kartavyāyāṃ yatau dṛtīyapāde tathā na kṛtamiti vaikalye 'pi svarasandhinimittatvānna doṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, even though in the second quarter the caesura that should be at the twelfth position has not been observed, since this is due to vowel <s>sandhi</s>, there is no fault.
An example of verb-defective (<s>kriyāvikala</s>) —
With your sword, O king, which is most adept at destroying the fourfold army of enemies,

children.text: bhūpāla tava khaḍgena vipado mānagarvitāḥ // Ckc_2.*32 //
children.translated_text: the calamities born of pride (are vanquished). // Ckc_2.*32 //

children.text:
atra nāmaśeṣakriyānta iti na vidyate /
tena kriyāvikalamidam /
evaṃ kārakādivikalamapyūhyam /
children.translated_text: Here, there is no verb ending the noun-phrase. Hence this is verb-defective (<s>kriyāvikala</s>). Similarly, deficiency of case-relations (<s>kārakavikala</s>) and the like should also be inferred.
This becomes a merit when it requires (a verb like) 'is' etc., or when it is self-sufficient (without one). // Ckc_2.27 //
As follows:
The <s>Rāmas</s> and King <s>Siṅgabhūpa</s> — these four are clearly portions of <s>Hari</s> (Viṣṇu);

children.text: samau tatra mahodāttau viṣamau tu mahoddhatau // Ckc_2.*33 //
children.translated_text: of these, two are equal (in being) greatly generous, and two are unequal (in being) greatly fierce. // Ckc_2.*33 //

children.text:
atra prathamārthe bhavantītyapekṣāyāṃ tadantarbhāvena vaikalye 'pi yatrānya kriyāpadaṃ nāsti tatrāsirbhavatirhi prathamapuruṣe prayujyata ityanuśāsanād guṇatvam /
dvītīyārdhe kriyābhāvepyudāttādi guṇasaṃbandhadyotakaniṣṭhāntatvena nirākāṅbhatvāt samarthakatvamiti guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, in the first meaning, when the verb 'are' is required, even though there is a deficiency due to its being subsumed (within the sentence), the grammatical rule states that the verb 'as' (to be) in the third person is employed where no other verb is present — hence it is a merit. In the second half, even without a verb, since the participial forms ending in adjectives like 'generous' etc. convey the relation of qualities and are self-sufficient without requiring (a verb) — this self-sufficiency constitutes a merit (<s>guṇa</s>).
But when it merely fails to manifest the cause of aesthetic wonder — that is called <s>kevala</s> (bare/plain). // Ckc_2.28 //
As follows:
Women look at the king, seated on a palanquin and arriving on the royal road,

children.text: striyaḥ paśyanti rājānaṃ puraḥ paścātparicchadam // Ckc_2.*34 //
children.translated_text: from the front and from behind at his retinue. // Ckc_2.*34 //

children.text: atra guṇādīnāṃ camatkārakāraṇānāmasphuṭatvena pratīteḥ jātimātravattiṣṭhatīti kevalamidam /
children.translated_text: Here, since the causes of aesthetic wonder — such as merits and the like — are only faintly perceived, the verse stands merely as a bare statement of its type — hence this is <s>kevala</s> (plain).
That plain (verse), when used in Vedic benedictions and the like, becomes a merit. // Ckc_2.29 //
As follows:
O King <s>Siṅgabhūpa</s>, may all the planets, along with the lunar mansions (<s>nakṣatra</s>),
always bestow upon you the fruits of the eleventh house, granting boons. // Ckc_2.*35 //
And as follows:

children.text: amī vediṃ paritaḥ kluptadiṣṇyāḥ samidvantaḥ prāntasaṃstīrṇadarbhāḥ /
children.translated_text: These (fires), arranged around the altar with their stations fixed, bearing sacrificial fuel, with <s>darbha</s> grass spread at the edges,

children.text: avaghnanto duritaṃ havyagandhair- vaitānāstvāṃ vahnayaḥ pālayantu // Ckc_2.*36 //
children.translated_text: dispelling sin with the fragrance of oblations — may these <s>vaitāna</s> (sacrificial) fires protect you. // Ckc_2.*36 //

In this and similar cases, even though the cause of aesthetic wonder is indistinct — making it plain (<s>kevala</s>) — since it is a benedictory verse of a pure Vedic ritualist, the sage <s>Kaṇva</s>, it is acceptable.
Thus (concludes) the examination of sentence-faults and sentence-merits.
<s>Śrīḥ</s>

children.text: iti sarasasāhityacāturīdhurīṇaviśveśvarakavīndracandra praṇītāyāṃ śrīsiṅgabhūpālakīrtisudhāsāraśītalāyāṃ camatkāracandrikāyāṃ dvitīyo vilāsaḥ //
children.translated_text: Thus, in the <s>Camatkāracandrikā</s>, composed by <s>Viśveśvara Kavīndracandra</s>, who is pre-eminent in the skill of elegant literary art, (a work) cool as the essence of the nectar of the fame of King <s>Siṅgabhūpāla</s> — (ends) the second <s>vilāsa</s> (chapter).
Third <s>vilāsa</s> (chapter)
<s>Camatkāracandrikā</s>, composed by <s>Viśveśvara Kavicandra</s> — third <s>vilāsa</s> (chapter).

children.text: artho vācyaśva lakṣyaśva vyaṅgayo 'pi ca vivicyate /
children.translated_text: Meaning (<s>artha</s>) is analyzed as <s>vācya</s> (denoted), <s>lakṣya</s> (indicated), and also <s>vyaṅgya</s> (suggested).
The meaning apprehended through the functions of denotation (<s>abhidhā</s>) — namely universals (<s>jāti</s>) and the like — is called <s>vācya</s> (denoted meaning). // Ckc_3.1 //

children.text: yathā dānena karṇo dayayā dilīpo nayena kāvyo vinayena rāmaḥ /
children.translated_text: As follows: "<s>Karṇa</s> in generosity, <s>Dilīpa</s> in compassion, <s>Kāvya</s> (Śukra) in statecraft, <s>Rāma</s> in modesty —

children.text: yadi prasiddhiṃ dadatāmamībhiḥ śrīsiṅgabhūpo nikhilaiḥ prasiddhaḥ // Ckc_3.*1 //
children.translated_text: even if these (worthies) were to confer renown, King <s>Siṅgabhūpa</s> is renowned through all (of these qualities combined)." // Ckc_3.*1 //

children.text: atra sarveṣāṃ padānāṃ jātyādivācakatvādarthasya vācyatvaṃ pratīyate /
children.translated_text: Here, since all words denote universals and the like (through their primary denotative function), the meaning is perceived as <s>vācya</s> (denoted).
The meaning apprehended through the function of indication (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) is called <s>lakṣya</s> (indicated meaning). // Ckc_3.2 //
The indicated meaning (<s>lakṣyārtha</s>) is of four kinds: (arising) from the incompatibility of the denoted meaning (<s>vācyārtha</s>) with that very (context) —

children.text: samavetaḥ saṃyuktaḥ sambandhī sadṛśa ṅatyuktaḥ // Ckc_3.3 //
children.translated_text: <s>Samaveta</s> (inherent) means conjoined; <s>saṃyukta</s> (connected) means related; <s>sadṛśa</s> (similar) is as stated. // Ckc_3.3 //

children.text: tatra samaveto lakṣyārtho yathā rājanyake pratibhaṭaṃ pratijanyaraṅge rudraṃ prakāśayati te saravālarekhā /
children.translated_text: There, the <s>samaveta lakṣyārtha</s> (inherently indicated meaning) is illustrated as follows, in a verse on the hero — in the arena against the rival, it shows <s>Rudra</s> in his line of arrows;

children.text: śrīsiṅgabhūpacakite śaraṇāgate 'smin padmekṣaṇaṃ vivṛṇute hi kaṭākṣarekhā // Ckc_3.*2 //
children.translated_text: when <s>Śrīsiṅgabhūpa</s> is alarmed, the refuge-seeker — his side-glance reveals the lotus-eyed one [<s>Viṣṇu</s>]. // Ckc_3.*2 //

children.text:
atra rudraśabdo mukhyārthe skhaladgatiḥ /
tena rudreṇāvinābhūtasya śatṛsaṃharaṇasāmarythasya lakṣaṇayā vivakṣitatvāt samavetalakṣyārthatvam /
children.translated_text: Here the word '<s>Rudra</s>' falters in its primary meaning; since the power to destroy enemies, which is inseparable from <s>Rudra</s>, is intended through indication (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>), it is a case of <s>samaveta-lakṣyārtha</s> (inherently indicated meaning).
The conqueror of various regions, upon entering his own city, <s>Kṣīsiṅgabhūpa</s>, having experienced the royal title —
the palace terraces on all sides scatter handfuls of flowers and ceremonial rice, preceded by cries of 'Victory!' // Ckc_3.*3 //

children.text:
atra saudhāṅgaṇānāmacetanānāṃ puṣpāñjaliparikṣepāsaṃbhavāt pure ca saudhabāhulyavivakṣayā tatsaṅgatāḥ paurāṅganāḥ lakṣyanta iti saṃyuktalakṣyārthatvam /
virodhyavirodhakabhāvādiramukhyaḥ sambandhaḥ /
tadvān sambandhī
children.translated_text: Here, since it is impossible for the insentient palace terraces to scatter flower-offerings, and since there is an intention to express the abundance of palaces in the city, the women of the city who are associated with them are indicated — thus it is a case of <s>saṃyukta-lakṣyārtha</s> (connected indicated meaning). The non-primary relationship is one of opposition-to-opposition etc. One who has such a relationship is <s>sambandhī</s> (relational).
As follows:

children.text: śrīsiṅgakṣitipālakaḥ prayatate yadyatsamāṭīkituṃ tattatpūrayituṃ cireṇa niyatirbaddhavratā tiṣṭhati /
children.translated_text: Whatever <s>Śrīsiṅgakṣitipālaka</s> (King <s>Siṅga</s>) endeavors to accomplish, Destiny (<s>niyati</s>) stands bound by a vow to fulfill it in due course;

children.text: asmāsu pratikūlatā tu jahatī bhūyāḥ kṛtārthodyamāḥ jāyethā śvirajīvanī pravasatā masmākamālirgirā // Ckc_3.*4 //
children.translated_text: may adversity toward us depart; may you be accomplished in your endeavors; may your long life prosper while dwelling away from us — [may you not take heed of] our words! // Ckc_3.*4 //

children.text:
atra niyatyā bhinnānāṃ ripubhūpatīnāṃ vanaṃ prati cirajīvinī bhūyā ityāśīrāśaṃsāsaṅgaterabhāvāt taddvirūddhaḥ śāparupārtho lakṣyate /
ādiśabdādavayavāvayavibhāvasaṃbandhādiryathā
children.translated_text: Here, since there is no coherence in the blessing that enemy kings, different from Destiny, should live long in the forest, the opposite meaning in the form of a curse is indicated, which contradicts that [apparent blessing]. The word '<s>ādi</s>' (etc.) includes the relationship of part and whole, etc. For example:

children.text: grīṣmo niḥśvasiteṣu locanayuge varṣāśśaradgaṇḍyor hemantassvasakhīmukheṣu śiśiro 'pyālepane vastuni /
children.translated_text: In her sighs, summer [is present]; in the pair of eyes, the rainy season; in the cheeks, autumn; in the faces of her companions, winter; in the cold season, in the ointment on the body —

children.text: caitrastalpavikalpanāsu vasati śrīsiṅgapṛthvīpate tvāṃ saṃsevitumāgateṣu dharaṇīpāleṣu tadyoṣitām // Ckc_3.*5 //
children.translated_text: in the arrangements of the bed, spring (<s>caitra</s>) dwells, O <s>Śrīsiṅgapṛthvīpati</s> (Lord <s>Siṅga</s>), when kings come to attend upon you, [all these seasons appear] in their women. // Ckc_3.*5 //

children.text:
atrāvayavibhūtartuprakramabhaṅgarūpānupapatteḥ tatparihārāya caitra iti pūrvāvayavenāvayavī vasanto lakṣyate /
sādaśyāllakṣyārtho yathā nāyakasyaiva
children.translated_text: Here, since there is an inconsistency in the disruption of the sequence of seasons as manifest realities, to resolve this, by the word '<s>caitra</s>' (the month), the whole — spring (<s>vasanta</s>) — is indicated through the part. The <s>lakṣyārtha</s> based on resemblance (<s>sādṛśya</s>) is illustrated for the hero himself:

children.text: kānte kṛtāgasi puraḥ parivartamāne sakhyaṃ sarojaśaśinoḥ sahasā babhūva /
children.translated_text: When the beloved, having transgressed, turns about before her, the friendship of the lotus and the moon suddenly came about;

children.text: rūkṣākṣaraṃ sudṛśi vaktumapārayantyām indīvaradvayamavāpa tuṣāradhārām // Ckc_3.*6 //
children.translated_text: unable to speak harsh words to the beautiful one, the pair of blue lotuses [her eyes] acquired a shower of dew-drops [tears]. // Ckc_3.*6 //

children.text: atra sarojādīnāṃ mukhyārthānanvayena tatsadṛśaḥ karatalādilakṣaṇārthaḥ sādṛśyanibandhanayā lakṣaṇayā lakṣyate /
children.translated_text: Here, since the primary meanings of 'lotus' etc. do not apply, the meaning resembling them — the palm of the hand, etc. — is indicated through the indication based on resemblance.
The suggested meaning (<s>vyaṅgyārtha</s>), accompanied by suggestion (<s>vyañjanā</s>), whether through word or meaning,
is characterized as substance (<s>vastu</s>), figure of speech (<s>alaṅkāra</s>), <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion), <s>bhāva</s> (transitory emotion), etc. // Ckc_3.4 //
The first [substance-type] is as follows:

children.text: līlālokanalolupaṃ mṛgakulaṃ gantā guhāntānimāṃ- statkpyagrasanavratīha bhavitā dvīpī ruṣīddīpitaḥ /
children.translated_text: "A herd of deer, eager to gaze playfully, is going to these cave interiors; there will be a leopard here, vowed to seize them in its jaws, enraged and inflamed;

children.text: yātā tanmṛgayā ratevanamidaṃ śrīsiṅgabhūpo rayād ityādirbhaya mādiśantyarinṛpāḥ strīṇāmanībhāvratam // Ckc_3.*7 //
children.translated_text: this forest has gone to hunt those deer" — thus do the enemy kings, in fear, teach the vow of fearlessness to the women of <s>Śrīsiṅgabhūpa</s>. // Ckc_3.*7 //

children.text: atra parilīnaśatrubhūvarā giriguhānāyakena nākrāntā iti yattadidaṃ durgaṃbuddhyā na bhavati kintu palāyitā nānuyātavadhyā iti manīṣayeti vastu vyajyate /
children.translated_text: Here, the fact that the hidden enemy lords were not pursued by the hero into the mountain caves is not because [the caves] were considered fortresses, but rather because those who had fled are not to be slain — this factual meaning (<s>vastu</s>) is suggested.
The second [figure-of-speech type] is as follows:

children.text: pṛthvīṃ śrīsiṅgabhūpe vahati phaṇavatāmīśitāraṃ pramodā- dākalpaṃ kelitalpaṃ kalayitumanasoradipuṃso nirodhe /
children.translated_text: While <s>Śrīsiṅgabhūpa</s> bears the earth, [<s>Śeṣa</s>], the lord of serpents, with delight, as a perpetual bed of sport to accomplish the desire of the supreme being, with the cessation of —

children.text: bhūmau bhāraprasaṅgātpunarapi patitā kelitalpāpadeśā- dākalpatvaikayogyaṃ bhujaga iti padaṃ gāyate khyātapūrvam // Ckc_3.*8 //
children.translated_text: having fallen to the ground again due to the weight, on the pretext of the bed of sport, sings the famous word '<s>bhujaga</s>' (serpent) as the only suitable one for perpetuity. // Ckc_3.*8 //

children.text:
atra nāyakasya sarveṣu rājasu sevakeṣu raṇābhāvādalabdhanavakapālasya kapālino jīrṇakapālamālikāsthāne bhūbhāraviyuktaṃ śeṣāhiṃ niveśayitukāmasya vetyutprekṣālahkāro vyajyate /
kiñca nāyakenaiva jagattrāṇabāra nirvahaṇādāśvastasya nārāyaṇasya nidrāmākāṅkṣata iveti ca tenaiva pratīyate /
children.translated_text: Here, the figure of <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) is suggested: since the hero has no new skull-bowls because there are no battles among all the servant-kings, [<s>Śiva</s>] <s>Kapālin</s> (the skull-bearer), in place of his garland of old skulls, wishes to install <s>Śeṣa</s> the serpent, freed from the burden of the earth. Furthermore, since the hero himself bears the burden of protecting the world, <s>Nārāyaṇa</s>, being reassured, seems to desire sleep — this too is perceived through the same [suggestion].
The third, in the form of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion), is as follows:

children.text: śrīsiṅgakṣitināyakasya ripavo dhāṭīkṣaterākulāḥ śuṣyattālupuṭaṃ skhalatpadatalaṃ vyālokayanto diśaḥ /
children.translated_text: The enemies of <s>Śrīsiṅgakṣitināyaka</s> (King <s>Siṅga</s>), terrified of his military assault, with parching palates, stumbling feet, looking toward the directions,

children.text: dhāvitvā kathamapyupetya tamasā gāḍhopagūḍhāṃ guhām anviṣyanti tadantare 'pi karasaṃsparśena gartāntaram // Ckc_3.*9 //
children.translated_text: having somehow run and reached a cave deeply embraced by darkness, they search even within it, by the touch of their hands, for a deeper pit. // Ckc_3.*9 //

children.text:
atra nāyakavirodhisamāśrayo bhayānako raso nijavibāvādibhirasaṃlakṣyakramatayā vyajyate /
bhāvarūpaścaturtho yathā nāyakasyaiva
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>bhayānaka rasa</s> (horrific/fearful aesthetic emotion), whose substrate is the enemies of the hero, is suggested through its own <s>vibhāvas</s> (determinants) etc. in an unmanifest manner. The fourth, in the form of <s>bhāva</s> (transitory emotion), is illustrated for the hero himself:
The friendship of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic) and <s>vīra</s> (heroic) [rasas]; the companionship of <s>māugdhya</s> (naivete) and <s>vaiyātya</s> (coquetry);
the union of <s>lāsya</s> (graceful dance) and <s>tāṇḍava</s> (vigorous dance) — let us worship that married couple! // Ckc_3.*10 //

children.text:
atra maugdyetyādau viruddhagaṇaghaṭanayā lāsyetyādau viruddhakriyāghaṭanayā dāmpatyamityatra viruddhajātighaṭanayā vācintyaiśvaryapratipādakor'dhanārīśvaralakṣaṇābhimatadaivatagaicaro vakturbhaktibhāvo vyajyate /
evamanyepyādiśabdagrāhyā rasabhāvādirūpā vyaṅyārthāstatratatrodāharaṇe draṣṭavyāḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, through the combination of opposed groups in '<s>māugdhya</s>' etc., through the combination of opposed actions in '<s>lāsya</s>' etc., and through the combination of opposed species in '<s>dāmpatya</s>' (married couple), the <s>bhakti-bhāva</s> (devotional emotion) of the speaker toward the intended deity characterized as <s>Ardhanārīśvara</s> (the half-male, half-female Lord), which establishes inconceivable sovereignty, is suggested. Thus other suggested meanings in the form of <s>rasa</s>, <s>bhāva</s>, etc. to be understood from the word '<s>ādi</s>' should be seen illustrated in various places.
<s>Apārtha</s> (meaningless), <s>vyartha</s> (purposeless), <s>ekārtha</s> (tautologous), <s>sasaṃśaya</s> (ambiguous), <s>apakrama</s> (disordered),
<s>paruṣa</s> (harsh), <s>virasa</s> (insipid), <s>bhinna</s> (inconsistent), <s>atimātra</s> (excessive), <s>anujjvala</s> (dull) — // Ckc_3.5 //
Now, the faults of meaning (<s>arthadoṣas</s>):
comparisons with the low, the superior, or the dissimilar; comparison with what is unfamiliar;

children.text: aślīlaṃ ca viruddhaṃ ca doṣāḥ kāvyārthagocarāḥ // Ckc_3.6 //
children.translated_text: <s>aślīla</s> (vulgar) and <s>viruddha</s> (contradictory) — these are the faults pertaining to the meaning of poetry. // Ckc_3.6 //
Here, in '<s>apārtham</s>' etc., the neuter gender should be understood from the designation of the predominance of the quality [rather than the object].
That which is devoid of collective meaning is called <s>apārtha</s> (meaningless). // Ckc_3.7 //
For example:

children.text: caitye śaṃbhorvadanadaśake vīkṣya dīrghaṃ karāgram matvā durgaṃ lavaṇadhanuṣe kāmadevāya huṃ phaṭ /
children.translated_text: Seeing the long finger-tips on the ten faces of <s>Śambhu</s> at the <s>caitya</s> (shrine), thinking it a fortress, [saying] to <s>Kāmadeva</s> (god of love) with the salt-bow — '<s>huṃ phaṭ</s>!'

children.text: ityārādhya praṇavamukhare prāñjalau pāraśīke tuṣṭā lakṣmīrvitarati śubhaṃ siṅgabhūpālakāya // Ckc_3.*11 //
children.translated_text: Thus worshipping, with a <s>Pāraśīka</s> (Persian) [attendant] offering salutation with joined palms and reciting <s>praṇava</s> (Om) — the pleased <s>Lakṣmī</s> bestows auspiciousness upon <s>Siṅgabhūpālaka</s>. // Ckc_3.*11 //
Here, the meaninglessness of the collective sense is quite evident, due to the mutual disconnectedness [of the elements].
In cases of agitated or mad speech, this [fault] becomes subordinate and serves as an ornament. // Ckc_3.8 //
In the case of agitation, for example:

children.text: ko vā jeṣyati somavaṃśatilakānasmān raṇaprāṅgaṇe hantāsmāsu parāṅmukho hatavidhiḥ kiṃ durgamadhyāsmahe /
children.translated_text: "Who will defeat us, the ornaments of the lunar dynasty, in the battle arena? Alas, fate has turned its back on us! Should we take refuge in a fortress?

children.text: asmatpūrvanṛpānayaṃ nihatavān dīrghān dhigasmadbhujān kiṃ vākyairanavotasiṅganṛpateḥ sevaiva kṛtyaṃ padam // Ckc_3.*12 //
children.translated_text: This one has slain our ancestors! Shame on our long arms! What use are words? The only proper course is service to King <s>Anavotasiṅga</s>." // Ckc_3.*12 //

children.text: atra vākyārthanāṃ parasparāsaṅgatatve 'pi nāyakajaitrayātrāsamākarṇanavyākulānāṃ pratyathibhūpānāṃ nānābhāvaśābalyasūcakatvād guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, even though the sentence-meanings are mutually disconnected, since they indicate the confusion of various emotions in the rival kings who are agitated upon hearing of the hero's military expedition, it becomes a virtue.
In the case of madness, for example:

children.text: autsukyādanavotasiṅganṛpaterākāramālikhya sā nirvarṇyāyamasau mama priya iti premābhiyogabhramāt /
children.translated_text: Having drawn the form of King <s>Anavotasiṅga</s> out of eagerness, examining it — 'This is my beloved!' — through the delusion of love's importunity,

children.text: āśūtthāya tatopasṛtya tarasā kiṃcidvivṛttānanā sāsūyaṃ sadarasmitaṃ sacarasmitaṃ sacakitaṃ sākāṅkṣamālaukate // Ckc_3.*13 //
children.translated_text: quickly rising and approaching it swiftly, with face slightly turned, she gazes with jealousy, with gentle smiles, with playful smiles, with startled looks, with longing. // Ckc_3.*13 //

Here, even though the meanings — the sudden rising, approaching, and changes in gaze directed at a painting — are disconnected and lack collective unity, since they indicate all the states of love that manifest the intensity of passion, it becomes a virtue.
What is said about a matter already expressed, or what would be purposeless — that is declared <s>vyartha</s> (purposeless). // Ckc_3.9 //
For example:

children.text: netrābhyāmavalokya siṅganṛpatiṃ dvābhyāṃ raṇe vidviṣaḥ savyūhairabhiyānti sapratibhaṭānālokya garvoddhatān /
children.translated_text: Having seen King <s>Siṅga</s> in battle with [their] two eyes, the enemies advance against him with their armies, seeing the proud rivals;

children.text: doṣṇā svena nijaṃ kṛpāṇamavate tatkhaḍgadhārāṃ gatās te svaḥstrīkucakumbhayormṛgamadaṃ lumpanti lumpanti ca // Ckc_3.*14 //
children.translated_text: with his own arm he takes up his own sword; those who have met his blade's edge plunder the musk from the bosoms of heavenly women, and plunder it again. // Ckc_3.*14 //

children.text:
atrāvalokyetyanenaiva netrābhyāmiti, netrābhyāmityanenaiva dvābhyāmiti doṣṇā kṛpāṇamavata ityanenaiva, svena nijamiti cārthasāmarthyādevāvagateḥ netrādīnāṃ gatārthatvam /
surastrīmṛgamadalepanakrīḍayaiva ripūṇāṃ kathāśeṣatvāvagateḥ svaḥstrīti śabdaśleṣasāmarthyalabdhanijastrīkucakumbhamṛgamadalepanakriyāyā aprayojanatvād vyarthatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, 'with two eyes' is redundant since 'having seen' already implies it; 'with two' is redundant since 'with eyes' implies it; 'his own' is redundant since 'with his arm he takes his sword' already implies ownership; and since from the power of meaning alone it is understood that the enemies' story ends with the sport of applying musk on the bosoms of heavenly women, the [additional mention of] applying musk on their own women's bosoms obtained through the power of verbal double-meaning is purposeless — hence it is <s>vyartha</s>.
This becomes a virtue when the entirety [of expression] is intentionally desired. // Ckc_3.10 //
For example:
With unmoving [glances] from majesty, accompanied by the fragrance of undisturbed modesty, swelling with delight, in the company of startled-doe gazes,
generous from eagerness, revealing the secrets of the waves of affection — with such side-glances, the young woman gazed upon <s>Siṅgakṣmāramaṇa</s> (King <s>Siṅga</s>). // Ckc_3.*15 //

Here, even though 'with side-glances' is redundant since 'the young woman gazed' already implies it without any other possibility, because it is employed to express the specific qualities of steadiness, modesty-fragrance, etc., it is not a fault. An example of purposelessness:

children.text: saṅkalpairanavotasiṅganṛpatau saṃrūḍhamūlāṅkurai- rākrāntā tanutāṃ gatā smaraśaraiśśāteva śātodarī /
children.translated_text: Invaded by the resolutions regarding King <s>Anavotasiṅga</s>, with well-rooted shoots, struck by the arrows of <s>Smara</s> (Love), she has grown thin, the slender-waisted one, as if cut;

children.text: asmannūlamidaṃ tanutvamiti kiṃ lajjālasai locane prāpte pakṣmapuṭāvṛtiṃ ratipatestat ketanaṃ jṛmbhatām // Ckc_3.*16 //
children.translated_text: "Is this thinness our root?" — as if [asking this], the eyes, languid with shame, having reached the state of being covered by the eyelid-sheaths, the banner of the Lord of Love is unfurled! // Ckc_3.*16 //

children.text: atra mīnavijṛmbhaṇakathanasya prakṛtāvasthānupayogitvenāprayojakatve 'pi loke prāyeṇa paribhūtānāṃ parābhaviturāpadaṃ vinā vijṛmbhaṇaṃ na saṃbhavatīti locanayorapunarunmīlanasūcanena navamāvasthāyāḥ parākāṣṭhā pratīyata iti guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, although the description of the fish-banner's unfurling is purposeless as it does not serve the state described in the main context, since in the world it is generally the case that the conquered cannot unfurl [their banner] without the defeat of the conqueror, by suggesting that the eyes will not open again, the extreme limit of the ninth state [of love-in-separation] is perceived — hence it becomes a virtue.
What has been stated [already] is <s>ekārtha</s> (tautologous) when the meaning is undifferentiated:
For example:

children.text: saṃrakṣitāṃ vetanamānanābhyāṃ karoti senāṃ vinihatya śatrūn /
children.translated_text: "He protects the army with honor and salary, having slain the enemies;"

children.text: kalyāṇabhūpo vinihatya śatrūn balāni saṃrakṣati vetanādyaḥ // Ckc_3.*17 //
children.translated_text: "King <s>Kalyāṇa</s>, having slain the enemies, protects the forces, giving salaries first." // Ckc_3.*17 //
Here, because the two halves of the verse do not have distinct intentions, it is tautologous.
But in cases of excess of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion), this becomes a virtue. // Ckc_3.11 //
For example:

children.text: kumāraśrīsiṅge jaladhiraśanāṃ śāsati mahīm amaryādādhvastāḥ patanapariṇāhapratibhuvaḥ /
children.translated_text: "When Prince <s>Śrīsiṅga</s> rules the earth girded by oceans,

children.text: adharmā nirmūlā narakaparipākapraṇidhayo vinaṣṭā duśceṣṭāḥ kalikaluṣaveśīparidhayaḥ // Ckc_3.*18 //
children.translated_text: transgressions of propriety are destroyed, along with those who ensure the extent of downfall; sins are uprooted, along with those whose intentions lead to the torment of hell;

children.text: atra dvitīyādiṣu pādeṣu bhinnārthatvābhāve 'pi kenacidadharmagandho 'pyasmaddeśe na vidyata iti trirvācā dharmapratiṣṭhāpakasvāmipakṣapātātiśayopakṣiptaṃ sodrekeṇa cetasābhihitatvād guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: wicked deeds are annihilated, along with those who wear the garb of the impurity of the <s>Kali</s> age." // Ckc_3.*18 //

Here, although the second and following verses lack distinct meaning, it becomes a virtue because the [repeated expression] — 'not even a trace of sin exists in our land' — is uttered three times with an overflowing heart of partisanship toward the master who establishes <s>dharma</s>.
That which gives rise to doubt is called <s>sasaṃśaya</s> (ambiguous). // Ckc_3.12 //
For example:
In the campaigns of <s>Śrīsiṅgabhūpa</s>, the enemies with diminished resources,

children.text:
atra hīnasādhanā vidviṣaḥ sālaśreṇiṃ prākārapaṅktimāśritya jīvanaṃ prāṇān tṛṇaṃ kurvate tṛṇāya manyanta ityarthaḥ /
athavā sālaśreṇiṃ vāṭikāmāśritya hīnasādhanāḥ tṛṇaṃ jīvanaṃ prāṇadhāraṇaṃ kurvata iti ca nāsatpratipakṣatvamasatpratipakṣatvaṃ ve 'ti saṃśayapratīteḥ sasaṃśayamidam /
children.translated_text: taking refuge in a <s>sāla</s>-row, make life a [mere] blade of grass. // Ckc_3.*19 //

Here, the meaning is: enemies with diminished resources, having taken refuge in <s>sālaśreṇi</s> (a row of <s>sāla</s> trees / a rampart-line), make their life — their <s>prāṇas</s> — [worthless as] a blade of grass. Alternatively: having taken refuge in a <s>sāla</s>-grove (<s>vāṭikā</s>), the resourceless ones 'make grass their livelihood' — i.e. barely sustain life. Since doubt arises as to whether the opposition is real or unreal, this is <s>sasaṃśaya</s> (ambiguous).
When the intention is to express excellence etc., this too carries the weight of a virtue. // Ckc_3.13 //
For example:

children.text: vāmāḥ śyāmā vaśīkartuṃ neśate siṅgabhūpatim // Ckc_3.*20 //
children.translated_text: Women whose speech rivals the cuckoo, whose eyes [rival] the lion, dark-complexioned and beautiful — they are unable to bring King <s>Siṅgabhūpati</s> under their spell. // Ckc_3.*20 //

children.text:
atra kokilaspardhinaḥ kokilasvaravat kalamadhurāssallāpā yāsāṃ tāḥ /
mṛgavairīṇi mṛgalocanatulyāni locanāni yāsāṃ tāḥ /
vāmāḥ ramyāḥ śyāmā yuvatayo nāyakaṃ vaśīkartuṃ neśate na śaktā ityanena strīvyasanamasya nāstīti /
uta kokilaspardhināṃ kākānāṃ sallāpa iva sallāpā yāsāṃ tāḥnāmāḥ vakrāḥ śyāmāḥ kālāṅgyaḥ enaṃ vaśīkartuṃ neśata ityanenānuttamāsu kākasvarāḍhyāsu strīṣu na ramanta iti kāmaśāstraparijñānamastīti vā sandehe ubhayathāpi nāyakotkarṣapratītiriti guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, 'those who rival the cuckoo' means those whose conversation is as melodiously sweet as the cuckoo's voice; 'deer-eyed' means those whose eyes are like those of a deer; '<s>vāmā</s>' means 'beautiful'; '<s>śyāmā</s>' means 'dark-complexioned young women' — they are 'unable to bring the hero under their control' — by this it is shown that he has no weakness for women. Alternatively, those whose conversation is like that of crows (rivals of cuckoos), who are crooked (<s>vāmā</s>), dark-bodied (<s>śyāmā</s>) — they cannot bring him under control — meaning he does not delight in base women who sound like crows — thus either he has knowledge of the <s>Kāmaśāstra</s> (science of love). In the ambiguity, both ways show the hero's excellence — hence it is a quality.
Where there is an inversion of the natural sequence, that is called <s>apakrama</s> (disorder). // Ckc_3.14 //
For example:
On the terrifying battlefield, the enemy kings, seeing King <s>Śrī Siṅga</s>'s prosperity,
perform consultations of departure-times with astrologers claiming universal sovereignty. // Ckc_3.*21 //

children.text: atra pūrvaṃ purānnirgatya pratipakṣabhūpaiḥ paśvādatikrāntaprayāṇalagnapariśodhanaṃ kriyata ityapakramatvam /

children.translated_text: In cases of paradoxical reasoning and the like, this is generally considered a quality. // Ckc_3.15 //
Here, the enemy kings first go out from their city and afterwards verify the auspicious time for their departure — this inversion of sequence constitutes <s>apakrama</s> (disorder).
For example:
"Afterwards you release your patience, O King <s>Śrī Siṅga</s>;

children.text: purastādeva muñcanti paurastyā bhūbhujaḥ kṣamāḥ // Ckc_3.*22 //
children.translated_text: but first the eastern kings release their lands." // Ckc_3.*22 //

children.text: atra pūrvabhāvino nāyakacitte titikṣāmokṣaṇasya hetoḥ, hetumataḥ paśvādbhāvinaḥ pratirājanijadeśamokṣaṇasya ca paurvāparyaviparyasādapakramatve 'pi nāyakatitikṣāmokṣaṇasya deśamokṣaṇalakṣaṇapratirājasādhvasoddīpanaprakāśanaparatvādadoṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, although there is <s>apakrama</s> (sequential inversion) since the hero's releasing of patience (the cause) comes later while the enemy kings' releasing of their territories (the effect) comes first — this is not a fault because the mention of the hero's releasing patience is meant to reveal that it causes the terrified enemy kings to abandon their territories.
That which has a directly harsh meaning is called <s>paruṣa</s> (harshness). // Ckc_3.16 //
For example:

children.text: gaṇaḍagrāvatale nipātayata vā gartāntare datta vā vyāghrāṇāṃ purataḥ parikṣipata vā vyākrośato bālakān /
children.translated_text: "Throw them down the mountain slope, or cast them into a pit, or hurl them before the tigers — the wailing children!

children.text: hantāmī parito vanaṃ mṛgayataḥ kṣmāpālacūḍāmaṇeḥ vartante bhavatībhiradya hivayaṃ sarve 'pi dahyāmahe // Ckc_3.*23 //
children.translated_text: Alas, these are the men of the king who is the crown-jewel of rulers, hunting in the surrounding forest — today all of us shall be burned!" // Ckc_3.*23 //

children.text: atra nāyakacamūdhāṭībhayena giriguhāsu līnānāṃ kulīnakuṭumbinīruddiśya bālakarodananivāraṇābhiprāyamātrāṇyapi pratyakṣe rūkṣārthānyakṣarāṇi gaditānīti paruṣatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, words that are harsh in their direct meaning are spoken — though only intended for the purpose of silencing the crying of children — by noble family women hiding in mountain caves out of fear of the hero's military expedition. Hence the harshness.
It becomes a quality when it serves as beneficial advice, or in the recollection of past events, and the like. // Ckc_3.17 //
As beneficial advice, for example:

children.text: asmadvakṣasijadvayātkimu sukhaṃ svardanti kumbhadvayaṃ pīyūṣaṃ kimu sāramasmadadharādasmādapasmāritam /
children.translated_text: "Is there greater pleasure from these two breasts of ours? Do your pitcher-like arms surpass them? Is the nectar-like sweetness of our lower lip overshadowed by that?

children.text: ko 'yaṃ vo janiteti sāhasarasān śrīvīrasiṅghaprabho saṃrambhādapasārayantyarinṛpān prauḍhāḥ pratītoktibhiḥ // Ckc_3.*24 //
children.translated_text: Who is this one who begot you?" — With bold and daring words, O lord <s>Śrī Vīra Siṅgha</s>, the proud women drive away the enemy kings. // Ckc_3.*24 //

children.text: atra māraṇaśūcanābhiprāyeṇa paruṣatve 'pi maraṇaparyavasāyī balavatā nāyakena virodhaḥ pariharaṇīya iti hitopadeśatvād guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, although there is harshness due to the intention of suggesting killing, since the message is beneficial advice — namely that conflict with a more powerful hero whose death would be the outcome should be avoided — it has the quality of beneficial counsel.
In the recollection of past events, for example:

children.text: yanmukto 'yamajihvikā priyasakhā tvatkhaḍgadhārāmukhād yo dṛṣṭo na ca taiḥ kirātahatakairdurgopahārodyataiḥ /
children.translated_text: "That this tongueless dear friend of yours was released from the edge of your sword, and was not seen by those wretched tribals who were intent on offering tribute from the fortress—

children.text: tacvanmaṅgala sūtravaibhava miti prastauti siṅgaprabhor dhāṭīsaṃbhramanaṣṭaduṣṭapatikā ñcaikāṃ striyaṃ bandhutā // Ckc_3.*25 //
children.translated_text: that is the glory of your auspicious marriage thread" — thus a female relative praises one woman whose wicked husband was lost in the confusion of <s>Siṅgaprabhu's</s> military raid. // Ckc_3.*25 //
Here, although the first half contains harshness, since it merely recounts a past event that has already occurred, it has quality.
That which has a tasteless meaning, stained by impropriety (<s>anaucitya</s>), is called <s>virasa</s> (tasteless/insipid). // Ckc_3.18 //
For example:
Hearing the deep, terrifying sounds of King <s>Siṅga's</s> battle-preparations, the rival kings, with parched palates, falling with stiffened legs,

children.text: saṃmuhyante śrutiṣu marutāṃ śailakāntāradeśe niryāntīṣu śrutipujasukhaṃ vaiṇavībhyo vapābhyaḥ // Ckc_3.*26 //
children.translated_text: become stupefied — even as, in the mountain forests, when the winds pass through bamboo groves, flute-like sounds emerge that are pleasing to the ears. // Ckc_3.*26 //
Here, the attention to the pleasure of hearing the wind through bamboo hollows is inappropriate for those fleeing in fear of the military raid — hence the tastelessness.
The subordination of a non-principal element should be recognized as its quality by the experts. // Ckc_3.19 //
For example:

children.text: kastūryā tatkapola dvayabhuvi makarī nirmitau prastutāyāṃ nirmitsūnāṃ svavakṣasyatiparicayācvatpraśasterupāṃśu /
children.translated_text: When she began to draw <s>makarī</s> (crocodile) marks with musk on both her cheeks — from excessive familiarity with her own breasts, in secret, about your fame,

children.text: vīra śrīsiṅgabhūpa tvadahitakubhujāṃ rājyalakṣmīsapatnī- mānavyājena lajjāṃ sapadi vidadhate svāvarodhāḥ pragalbhāḥ // Ckc_3.*27 //
children.translated_text: O heroic King <s>Śrī Siṅga</s>, the bold women of the enemy's evil-armed queens, the co-wives of royal fortune, suddenly experience shame through pretense. // Ckc_3.*27 //

children.text: atra pratināyakagatā nāyakabirudavilekhananimittayā janitā svāvarodhasānnidhyādibhiruddīpitā lajjānumitaiḥ nirvedadainyaviṣādādibhirabhivyaktā nirvedadainyaviṣādādibhirupacitā tadanu tadanumitaireva mānasikakutsādibhirabhivyaktā nijajīvitajugupsā ca svāvarodhaviṣayā tatprāgalbhūyādibhiruddīpitā makarikātapatranirmāṇadibhirabhivyaktā tadanumitaiḥ harṣādibhirupacitā ratiśva nirbharamekatra saṃniveśita ityanaucityena virasatve 'pi tayornāyakabirudavileśanahetutayā nāyakakṛpākaṭākṣaprasāda sampannatayā ca na saṃbhāvyamānayośśaraṇāgatarakṣaṇalakṣaṇanāyakagataparopakāratvenā prādhānyādaduṣṭatvam //
children.translated_text: Here, though the shame of enemy queens generated by the hero's title-inscription, the disgust at their own lives aroused by intimacy with their own attendants, and erotic sentiment are all crowded together in apparent impropriety resulting in tastelessness — since these are subordinate to the hero's quality of protecting those who seek refuge (as the queens' shame and self-disgust stem from their husbands' defeat by the hero), the non-principal elements being subordinated is not a fault.
Where the initial mode of expression is not carried through to completion, the wise call it <s>bhinna</s> (broken). // Ckc_3.20 //
For example:
Languid from drinking <s>Gauḍī</s> wine, with jasmine garlands slipping from their loosened hair, with speech stumbling through pretense, beauties who are the jewels of their hair-parts,

children.text: tāruṇyodadhiśīkarā smarakalāsāmrājyasiddhikriyāḥ śrīsiṅgakṣitipāla tāvakaguṇān gāyanti gauḍāṅganāḥ // Ckc_3.*28 //
children.translated_text: sprays from the ocean of youth, empresses of the arts of <s>Smara</s> (Love) — O King <s>Śrī Siṅga</s>, the women of <s>Gauḍa</s> sing your virtues. // Ckc_3.*28 //

Here, since the initial mode of describing a type of intoxicated woman is not carried through with the continuation of quality-description such as 'madavatī' etc., it constitutes quality (of the <s>bhinna</s> type).

children.text: asyāpi guṇatā kvāpi yadi chāyā na hīyate // Ckc_3.21 //
children.translated_text: Even this is considered a quality sometimes, if the overall sense is not diminished. // Ckc_3.21 //

children.text: yathā grīṣmo niḥśvasiteṣu locanayuge varṣāḥ śaradgaṇḍayoriti pūrvodāhṛteṣu ṛtuṣvekavacanaprakramasya varṣā iti bahuvacanopādānād bhinnatve 'pi bhūmnyeva varṣā ityanuśāsanād bahuvacanaśruterapyarthaikyasyātyājyatvādekavacanachāyā na hīyata iti guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: For example, in the previously cited verse 'Summer in the breaths, the Rains in the eyes, Autumn in the cheeks' — although there is a break in the singular-number convention when 'varṣā' (rains) is used in the plural, since grammatical teaching affirms that the rains are referred to in the plural for abundance, the singular sense is not diminished — hence it is a quality.
That which is unbelievable and excessive is called <s>atimātra</s> (exaggeration). // Ckc_3.22 //
For example:
O King <s>Śrī Siṅga</s>, the force of the sighs of your enemies
makes the mountain forests bare — with their groves burned, with their boulders scattered all around. // Ckc_3.*29 //
Here, the range of the sighs of enemy kings — even if very hot and very numerous from the burden of defeat — is unbelievable in causing such burning and scattering. Hence it is exaggeration.
Some justify its quality-status as before;
others say it is delightful (<s>sarasa</s>) in accordance with worldly convention. // Ckc_3.23 //
The first type, for example:

children.text: śrīsiṅgakṣitipāla tāvakacamūdhāṭīṣu vājichaṭā riṃkhoddhūtarajobhirambunidhayo viśve 'pi gādhīkṛtāḥ /
children.translated_text: O King <s>Śrī Siṅga</s>, during your army's marches, the groups of horses, with the dust raised by their prancing, have made all the oceans shallow;

children.text: cañcatketupaṭāntavāntapavanair bhūyopyagādhīkṛtāḥ bhadre bhendramadāmbunā punaramī pūrvādhikaṃ pūritāḥ // Ckc_3.*30 //
children.translated_text: by the winds blown from the fluttering edges of the banners, they are made even more shallow; but alas! by the rut-water of the excellent elephants, these same oceans are once again filled even more than before! // Ckc_3.*30 //

children.text: atra senāvājirajasā samudrāṇāṃ śoṣaṇa sthalīkaraṇādiratimātratve 'pi punarapivāripūrakalpanayā vastusthiteravirodhād gāḍhamārgānuvartināṃ vidagdhānāmatiguṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, although the drying up and shallowing of the oceans by the dust of the army's horses is exaggeration, since the additional detail of refilling them with water restores consistency with reality, for discerning readers following the elaborate style, it has super-quality.
The second type, for example:

children.text: yātreyaṃ kuladevatāsu kimutodvāhakramo bhūbhujām ācārā nu sakhīti vā pratipataṃ vadhvā vivāhotsave /
children.translated_text: "Is this a pilgrimage to the clan-deity? Or is this the wedding procession of kings? Or is this the practice of greeting a friend?" — thus at every step, at the wedding celebration, the bride asks;

children.text: dhāṭīsaṃśravaṇā tpalāyanavatāṃ śrīsiṅgabhūpadviṣāṃ rājñāṃ marmanikṛntane paṭutarā tanmaṇḍalāgrādapi // Ckc_3.*31 //
children.translated_text: the words of the fleeing kings of <s>Śrī Siṅga's</s> enemies, who flee upon hearing of the military raid, are sharper in cutting the vital parts of those kings' circles than even their weapons. // Ckc_3.*31 //

children.text:
atra vācāṃ khaḍgādapi hṛdayamarmabhedakathanā datimātratve 'pi tādṛśānāṃ tādṛśāni vacanāni vajrādapi hṛdayamarmāṇi bhindanti /
kimuta khaḍgādiriti lokasthiteranuvartanādvidarbhamārgānusāriṇāṃ dākṣiṇātyānāmatiguṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, although the statement that words are sharper than swords in piercing the heart's vital points is exaggeration, since the worldly saying is that 'such words pierce the vital points of the heart more than even a thunderbolt, let alone a sword' — for southern poets following the <s>Vidarbha</s> style, this confirms the exaggeration as a quality.
That which does not clearly sparkle with <s>camatkāra</s> (wonder) is called <s>anujjvala</s> (lacking brilliance). // Ckc_3.24 //
For example:

children.text: kroḍān khananti vipine bhakṣayanti mṛgān kuśān /
children.translated_text: They dig for roots in the forest, they eat wild animals and grasses;
they sleep in the shade of trees — the enemies of King <s>Kalyāṇa</s>. // Ckc_3.*32 //

children.text: atra vidviṣāṃ nagareṣu bhayavyākulatayā kadācidapi nidrā cakṣuḥ nopaiti bhraṣṭarājyāstu kāntāre vanyajantuvat visrabdhā nidrāntīti vivakṣitasyāpi camatkārasyātikleśena pratīte rasphuṭālaṅkāratvāccānujjvalatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, though the intended meaning — that the enemies, unable to sleep in their own cities due to fear, now sleep securely in the wilderness like wild animals after losing their kingdoms — has wonder, it is perceived only with great difficulty due to the absence of clear ornamentation. Hence it lacks brilliance.

children.text: vidagdhahṛdayāḥ vkāpi tasyāpi guṇatāṃ viduḥ // Ckc_3.25 //
children.translated_text: Discerning hearts sometimes recognize its quality. // Ckc_3.25 //

children.text:
yathā "sarve grahā sanakṣatrā" ityādi pūrvodāhṛtam /
atra jātyādyarthālaṅkāraviraheṇānujjvalatve 'pi śuddhaśrotriyāśīrvādānukaraṇatvād guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: For example, the previously cited 'All planets with their constellations...' — though lacking brilliance due to the absence of ornamental figures like <s>jāti</s> and others, since it imitates the form of a pure Vedic blessing, it has quality.
That which obviously has a lowly standard of comparison and the like is identified by its very name. // Ckc_3.26 //
An example with a lowly or excessive standard of comparison:
O King <s>Śrī Siṅga</s>, beholding the edge of your sword, with its razor-sharp blade keener than a kuśa-grass tip,

children.text: līnāḥ praviśya vipinaṃ pradarāntarālaṃ nārāyaṇodaradarīmiva vairibhūpāḥ // Ckc_3.*33 //
children.translated_text: the enemy kings, hiding, enter the depths of mountain caves as if entering the cave of <s>Nārāyaṇa's</s> belly. // Ckc_3.*33 //

children.text: atra khaḍgadhārāṃ prati kuśadhārāyāmatiniśātatve nīcatvādatinīcopamānatvaṃ vipinapradaraṃ prati vaipulyena nārāyaṇodarasyātyādhikyādadhikopamānatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, the kuśa-grass blade as a comparison for the sword's edge is a lowly standard because of its excessive inferiority in sharpness; and the cave of <s>Nārāyaṇa's</s> belly as a comparison for a mountain cave is an excessive standard due to its vastly superior magnitude.
An example with a dissimilar standard of comparison:
King <s>Kalyāṇa</s>, with bow drawn in a circle on the battlefield,
with a water-lily trembling in his hand, shines like <s>Mīnāṅka</s> (the Moon, marked with a fish). // Ckc_3.*34 //
Here, there is no basis of similarity between the bow and the <s>saugandhika</s> (water-lily) — hence it is a dissimilar standard of comparison.
Even the first two types sometimes have quality, through the poet's skill. // Ckc_3.27 //
For example:
King <s>Siṅga</s>, to his opponent, takes a trifle of wealth like Mount <s>Kanaka</s> (Gold Mountain);

children.text: pātre tiṣṭhati purataḥ tṛṇakaṇavacyajati kanakāni // Ckc_3.*35 //
children.translated_text: when a worthy recipient stands before him, he discards heaps of gold like a particle of straw. // Ckc_3.*35 //

Here, although Gold Mountain and straw-particle are excessively high and low standards of comparison, since they intend to express the hero's supreme indifference in acquiring and discarding wealth, they are not faulty.
The dissimilar standard of comparison, in <s>vyatireka</s> (contrast) and <s>upamā</s> (simile) figures—
for example:

children.text: avivekī na surabhivat cintāmaṇiriva na yāti kāṭhinyam /
children.translated_text: Unlike the wish-fulfilling cow, he does not lack discrimination; unlike the wish-fulfilling gem, he does not attain hardness;
King <s>Śrī Siṅga</s>, the crest-jewel of kings — O <s>Śiva</s>, <s>Śiva</s>! — is the good fortune of the earth-world's fortune. // Ckc_3.*36 //
Here, though the comparison and compared are dissimilar, since it serves as a standard for the <s>vyatireka</s> (contrast) figure, it has quality.
An unfamiliar standard of comparison constitutes <s>aprathita-upama</s> (unknown simile). // Ckc_3.28 //
For example:
Alas! With hands like <s>saugandhika</s> (water-lily), with feet like blooming red lotus,
the women of <s>Gurjara</s> are shattered by the military raids of King <s>Śrī Siṅga</s>. // Ckc_3.*37 //

children.text: atra saugandhikakokanadayoḥ kāntākaracaraṇopamānatvena kaviprayogeṣu na prasiddhiriti duṣṭatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, <s>saugandhika</s> and <s>kokanada</s> (red lotus) are not well-known in poetic usage as standards of comparison for women's hands and feet — hence the fault.
Even this sometimes has quality, when the <s>camatkāra</s> (wonder) is stirred. // Ckc_3.29 //
For example:
O King <s>Śrī Siṅga</s>, the rows of arrows discharged by you, falling on all sides
around the necks of the enemy hero-kings in battle, are like garlands of a celestial maiden's <s>svayaṃvara</s> (self-choice ceremony). // Ckc_3.*38 //

children.text: atra nārājapaṅiktasvayaṃvaraṇasrajorupameyopamānabhāvāprasiddhāvapi surāṅgānāṃ bhoga hetutvasāmyācchamatkārātisya iti guṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, although the comparison between rows of arrows and self-choice garlands is unfamiliar, since the similarity lies in both being the cause of enjoyment (of celestial pleasures after death in battle) and the <s>camatkāra</s> is stirred — it has quality.
That which produces the perception of impropriety is designated <s>aślīla</s> (obscene/improper). // Ckc_3.30 //
For example:
Inflamed by battle, O king, your enemies—
they rise up and bend down in their boldness to strike at the opening. // Ckc_3.*39 //

children.text: atra prahāroddīpanaṃ randhraprahārāya namanonnamane ca śiśne 'pi vidyete iti tatpratīteraślīlatvam /
children.translated_text: Here, the rising and bending down for striking at the opening — since these are also found in the male organ — the suggestion of the obscene is perceived; hence it is <s>aślīla</s> (obscene).
Even this should be recognized as a literary quality when it is adopted by great poets and the like. // Ckc_3.31 //
For example —

children.text: jitvā tatpariraṃbhaṇa prakṛtikaṃ dyūte sakhīnāṃ puraḥ śāryāropaṇasūcite paṇavidhau śrīsiṅgabhūmībhujā /
children.translated_text: Having won the natural embrace as a wager in a game of dice before her friends, in the betting procedure indicated by the placing of <s>śārī</s> (game pieces), by King <s>Śrīsiṅgabhūbhuj</s> —
with her gaze wandering to her face from the waves of beauty on her gently smiling cheeks, with perspiring fingers, the beloved prepares the set of game pieces. // Ckc_3.*40 //

children.text:
atra śārikāstryupari śārikāropaṇena pumbhāvakelirūpasyāślīlasya pratīteraślīlatve 'pi kavibhirevaṃvidhasyāslīlasyāṅgīkārād guṇatvam /
kutra kavibhirevamurarīkṛtamiti cettarhi sādhu sarvato nidarśayāmaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, the placing of <s>śārikā</s> pieces upon the woman — though the perception of the obscene in the form of sexual play is <s>aślīla</s> — since such obscenity has been accepted by poets, it possesses literary quality. If asked where poets have thus accepted it, we shall demonstrate this well from all sources.

children.text: tadānanaṃ mṛtsurabhi kṣitīśvaro rahasyupāghrāya na tṛptimāyayau // Ckc_3.*41 //
children.translated_text: The lord of the earth, having secretly smelled that face fragrant with earth, did not reach satisfaction. // Ckc_3.*41 //
Thus indeed —
— thus in the <s>Raghuvaṃśa</s>.
With hair-graspings that tormented the moon (face), with nails straying from the proper path, with jealousy,
that love-play of <s>Pārvatī</s>, with loosened girdle-strings, was for the sake of insatiability. // Ckc_3.*42 //
— thus in the <s>Kumārasaṃbhava</s>.
With face-centered (kisses), with slow initial throat-embraces, with limbs quickly pressed together,

children.text: karapracāraiḥ śithiloparodhairlabdhaiḥ priyāyā mumude mukundaḥ // Ckc_3.*43 //
children.translated_text: with hand-movements of loosened resistance — <s>Mukunda</s> delighted in those obtained from his beloved. // Ckc_3.*43 //
— thus in the <s>Kandarpasaṃbhava</s>.
By her who had loosened her undergarment, casting away the upper cloth, clinging to her girdle,
with the weight of her broad breasts pressed in a circle — the lord of her heart embraced his beloved. // Ckc_3.*44 //
— thus in <s>Bhāravi</s>'s poem.
With gaze half-closed, quickly grasping the tip of the beloved's hand upon her loosened undergarment,
she cooed beautifully with a circular resonance, the lower lip-string struck by the reed-player of passion. // Ckc_3.*45 //
— thus in <s>Māgha</s>'s poem. The same should be understood in other works as well.
That which contradicts place, time, the arts, popular convention, logic, and authoritative treatises
is declared as <s>viruddha</s> (contradictory) by those who know the essence and life-breath of literature. // Ckc_3.32 //
Regarding place: <s>Āndhra</s>, <s>Mahārāṣṭra</s>, and the like. Regarding time: night and day, etc.
Song-forms, statecraft, and the like are arts (<s>kalā</s>); those relating to <s>kāma</s> (desire) and <s>artha</s> (wealth) are their domains. // Ckc_3.33 //

children.text:
carācarāṇāṃ bhūtānāṃ pravṛttirloka ucyate /
nyāyastu hetuvidyār yādāgamo dharmasaṃhitā // Ckc_3.34 //
children.translated_text: The behavior of all beings, moving and unmoving, is called <s>loka</s> (popular convention). <s>Nyāya</s> (logic) is the science of reasoning; <s>āgama</s> (authoritative treatise) is the compendium of <s>dharma</s>. // Ckc_3.34 //
Examples of contradiction with place and the rest —

children.text: rādhe māsi divāniśaṃ mṛgamadavyālepino mālatī śayyāyāṃ yamunātaraṅgapavanasparśotsukairvatsalaiḥ /
children.translated_text: In the month of <s>Rādha</s> (Vaiśākha), day and night, anointed with musk, on a bed of <s>mālatī</s> (jasmine), eager for the touch of the <s>Yamunā</s> river breeze, with affectionate ones,

children.text: dhātrīnāyakasevanāya militā bhūmīśvarā mānino rājādrau maṇihārasaurabhamayaiḥ krīḍhanti bandījanaiḥ // Ckc_3.*46 //
children.translated_text: the proud kings, assembled for the service of the patron lord, play on the royal mountain with captive attendants amid the fragrance of jewel-garlands. // Ckc_3.*46 //

children.text:
atrāndhradeśe yamuneti deśanirodhaḥ /
rādhemāsi mālatīśayyeti kālavirodhaḥ /
hārāṇāṃ saurabhamiti lokavirodhaḥ /
ete pratyakṣavirodhāḥ /
māninaḥ sovā militā iti svavacanavirodhaḥ /
bandijanā vatsalā ityaucityavirodhaḥ /
anyasevakānāmaharniśaṃ krīḍeti yuktivirodhaḥ /
ete anumānavirodhāḥ /
bandīkṛtaiḥ paraparigrahaiḥ krīḍantīti karmasaṃhitāvirodhaḥ /
bandīṣvanyāsakteḥ vyasanamapakṛtastrīṣu viśvāsaścetyarthāgamavirodhaḥ /
grīṣme divāniśaṃ krīḍanaṃ pakṣādvarṣanidāghayorityāyurvedavirodhaḥ /
grīṣme kastūrikāvilepanaṃ bhogaśāstravirodhaḥ /
atrāgamāntarbhūtānāmapi kalāśāstrāṇāṃ pṛthagabhidhānaṃ tadjñānasya sāhitye prādhānyajñāpanārtham /
children.translated_text: Here, '<s>Yamunā</s>' in the <s>Āndhra</s> region is a contradiction of place. 'In the month of <s>Rādha</s>, a <s>mālatī</s> bed' is a contradiction of time. 'Fragrance of garlands' is a contradiction of popular convention. These are contradictions perceptible to direct observation. 'Proud ones assembled' is a contradiction of one's own statement. 'Captive attendants being affectionate' is a contradiction of propriety. 'Servants of others playing day and night' is a contradiction of reasoning. These are contradictions inferred through reasoning. 'Playing with captives who are others' wives' is a contradiction of moral codes. 'Attachment to captive women being a vice, and trust in wronged women' is a contradiction of treatises on wealth and desire. 'Playing day and night in summer' contradicts the medical precept that (intercourse should be limited) in summer and rainy season. 'Musk-anointing in summer' contradicts the treatises on pleasure. Here, though the arts-treatises are included within the category of <s>āgama</s> (authoritative texts), their separate mention is for the purpose of indicating the primacy of their knowledge in literary composition.
When there is an intention to convey great portents, extraordinary power, and the like, this (contradiction) becomes a quality. // Ckc_3.35 //
An example when the intention is to describe a portent —

children.text: uddaṇḍapratigaṇḍabheravavibho smere kaṭākṣe ruṣā jāte kokanadacchavipratibhaṭe rāṣṭreṣu vidveṣiṇām /
children.translated_text: When the sidelong glance of the fierce lord <s>Uddaṇḍapratigaṇḍabhairava</s> (<s>Śrīsiṅga</s>), smiling with anger, appeared lotus-red against the enemy kingdoms,

children.text: mākandāśśarati prabhūtakalikāḥ padmaṃ kukūlodare pāṣāṇāḥ prahasanti hanta dadhate sandhyāsu nidrā dvijāḥ // Ckc_3.*47 //
children.translated_text: the mango trees shower abundant buds, lotuses bloom in furnace-bellies, stones burst into laughter, and at twilight the birds fall asleep! // Ckc_3.*47 //

children.text:
atra śaradi mākandaprasūnānīti kālavirodhaḥ /
kukūlodare padmamiti yuktivirodhaḥ pāṣāṇāḥ prahasantīti lokavirodhaḥ /
tadeṣāṃ duṣṭatve 'pi nāyakakopajaniṣyamāṇaparāṣṭravipattisūcakaturnimittavivakṣayā guṇatvam /

children.translated_text: An example when the intention is to describe extraordinary influence (<s>anubhāva</s>) —
Seeing the gardens on the royal mountain, now rendered unlovely, with their grounds frequented by herds of musk deer and their rows of camphor trees,

children.text: vismerā hṛdi pañcavarṇakaśukādākarṇya karṇotsavaṃ śrīsiṅgakṣitipālavikramakalāṃ nandantyapūrve janāḥ // Ckc_3.*48 //
children.translated_text: amazed at heart upon hearing the delightful sounds of the five-colored parrots, the people marvel at the unprecedented prowess of King <s>Śrīsiṅga</s>. // Ckc_3.*48 //
