children.text: atra nāyakaguṇādinā vasantādinā ca samuddīpitā vilāsinīnāṃ rativāsanā muhurmuhurvalitakaṣṭhakaṭākṣalakṣaṇena ca śarīrārambhānubhāvenānubadhyata iti tathoktto 'yam /
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>rati-vāsanā</s> (latent impression of love) of the beautiful women, kindled by the hero's qualities and by the spring season, is repeatedly bound by the bodily consequent of difficult sidelong glances — hence this is so called.

An example of <s>anubandha</s> characterized by the connection with multiple <s>anubhāvas</s>: With sweat-drops risen, with gentle smiles crushed, with horripilation breaking forth, with throat choked—
the limbs of the beautiful women, overpowered by the bodiless god of Love, (trembled) at the glance of the lord of the earth, King <s>Śrī Siṅga</s>. // Ckc_5.*5 //

children.text:
atra nāyakagocarā tadānīntanī purātanī vā vilāsinīnāṃ ratiḥ nāyakavilokanādibhiruddīpitā mandahāsena śarīrāraṃbheṇa svedādibhiśca sācvikaiḥ bahubhiranubadhyata iti tathoktaḥ /
sañcāriṇo nāma virvedaviṣādadainyaglāniśramamadagarvaśaṅkātrāsāvegonmādāpasmāravyādhi mohamaraṇālasyajaḍatā vrīḍāvahitthāsmṛtivitarkacintāśca matidhṛtiharṣotsukatvogratāmarṣakṛpāsūyācāpalyanidrāsuptibodhāśceti trayastriṃśat /
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>rati</s> (love) of the beautiful women directed toward the hero — whether present or past — kindled by the hero's glance and such excitants, is bound by numerous <s>sāttvika</s> responses: gentle smile (a bodily consequent), perspiration, and others. Hence it is so called. The <s>vyabhicāri bhāvas</s> (transient emotions) are: disgust, dejection, depression, fatigue, weariness, intoxication, pride, apprehension, fear, agitation, insanity, epilepsy, sickness, delusion, death, lethargy, stupor, shame, dissimulation, recollection, deliberation, anxiety, constancy, fortitude, joy, eagerness, fierceness, envy, compassion, jealousy, fickleness, drowsiness, dreaming, and awakening — thirty-three in all.
An example of <s>anubandha</s> with a single transient emotion:
In the spring pavilion of pleasure, amidst the tinkling of <s>Mādhava's</s> (Spring's) anklets and the murmuring of bees,

children.text: śrīsiṅgabhūmipatisaṅgatikāṅkṣiṇī sā hastāmbuje kṛtavatī nijagaṇḍapālim // Ckc_5.*6 //
children.translated_text: she who longed for the company of King <s>Śrī Siṅga</s> placed on her lotus-hand her own cheek. // Ckc_5.*6 //

children.text:
atra nāyakagocarā nāyikārativāsanā vāsantikādibhiruddīpitā karatalakapolavinyāsalakṣaṇaśarīrāraṃbhanijānubhāvānumitena cintālakṣaṇena vyabhicāriṇānu badhyata iti so 'yaṃ tathoktaḥ /
kecidenāṃ rasoktimekānubhāvavadekavyabhicāriṇo nibandhe sambandha eka eveti sphurattoktimevācakṣate /
vayaṃ punaetasyāmuktyāṃ sānubhāvena vyabhicāriṇaikassaṃbandhaḥ /
vyabhicāriṇā sthāyino dvitīya iti paraṃparayā saṃbandhānugatisaṃbhavādanubandhamāmanāma /
children.translated_text: Here, the heroine's <s>rati-vāsanā</s> toward the hero, kindled by the spring season and such, is bound by the transient emotion of <s>cintā</s> (anxiety), inferred from the bodily consequent of resting the cheek on the palm. Some consider this to be merely <s>sphurattā</s> (manifestation) rather than <s>anubandha</s>, since there is only one <s>anubhāva</s> and one transient emotion. We, however, consider it <s>anubandha</s> because the transient emotion connects with the consequent, and through the consequent connects with the permanent emotion, establishing a chain of successive connections.
Even when there is abundance of transient emotions, others call it this same thing (<s>anubandha</s>);

children.text: sa bakṣyamāṇo niṣpatterbheda eveti me matam // Ckc_5.17 //
children.translated_text: it is my view that it is indeed a type of <s>niṣpatti</s> (fruition) about to be described. // Ckc_5.17 //
For example:
A certain deer-eyed beautiful woman, delighting the eyes, seeing King <s>Śrī Siṅga</s>, the beloved of the earth,

children.text: ālokate pratidiśaṃ kuste svanindā- mālaṃbate karatalena kapolapātim // Ckc_5.*7 //
children.translated_text: gazes in every direction, takes hold of self-reproach, and places her hand on her cheek. // Ckc_5.*7 //

children.text:
atra parito vilokanena śaṅkā /
svanindopālaṃbhanena lāvaṇyagatirnirvedaḥ /
kapolakaratalasaṃsargeṇa cintā ca pratīyate /
atrānubhāvasaṃsargābhāve 'pi rateranubhāvotpādenānubandhadaśāyāmiva saṃcāribhāvabāhulyadaśāyāṃ vāsanāvāsantikādibhiruddīpitāyā iva pāṭavaviśeṣajanyatvādrasasya caturaśratayāpratibhānācca nivṛttireveyaṃ nānubandhamātramiti sulabham /
children.translated_text: Here, through looking around in all directions, <s>śaṅkā</s> (apprehension) is perceived; through self-reproach, <s>nirvedaḥ</s> (despondency) regarding her own beauty; through touching cheek with palm, <s>cintā</s> (anxiety). Here, even in the absence of connection with <s>anubhāvas</s>, since the profusion of transient emotions — generated by the special skill of the <s>rati</s> (love) kindled by the hero's qualities and the spring season — constitutes a distinctive state of rasa, this is <s>niṣpatti</s> (fruition), not mere <s>anubandha</s> (continuity).
Through the combination of <s>vibhāvas</s> (determinants), <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequents), <s>sāttvika</s> (involuntary responses), and <s>vyabhicārins</s> (transient emotions),
the well-rounded splendor of <s>rasa</s> — that is celebrated as <s>niṣpatti</s> (fruition). // Ckc_5.18 //
For example:

children.text: dṛṣṭvā siṅgavibhuṃ guṇaikavasatiṃ kācitkuraṅgekṣaṇā svinnāṅgī madhurasmitā pulakavatyārecitabhrūlatā /
children.translated_text: Seeing King <s>Siṅga</s>, the sole abode of virtues, a certain deer-eyed woman — perspiring, with a sweet smile, covered with horripilation, with eyebrow-creepers arched,

children.text: dhattevepathumākulāṃ kalayate sācīkarotyānanaṃ pāṇibhyāṃ vidadhāti gaṇḍayugalīmāliṅgati svāṃ sakhīm // Ckc_5.*8 //
children.translated_text: bearing a tremor, agitated, turning her face sideways, placing both palms on her cheeks, embracing her friend. // Ckc_5.*8 //

children.text: atra nāyakagocarā nāyikāratistatsānnidhyādinā dīpyamānā smitabhrūlatārecanalakṣaṇābhyāṃ śarīrāraṃbhānubhāvābhyāṃ svedapulakavepathulakṣaṇaissātvikairākulībhāvamukhasācīkaraṇakapolapidhānasakhīsamāliṅganānumitaiḥ sādhvasalajjāvahitthācāpalalakṣaṇaiḥ saṃcāribhāvaiḥ saṃskṛtetīyaṃ ratirūpeṇa rasasya niṣpattiḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, the heroine's <s>rati</s> directed toward the hero, being kindled by his proximity and such, is manifested through two bodily consequents (smile and eyebrow-raising), through the <s>sāttvika</s> responses of perspiration, horripilation, and trembling, and through the transient emotions of timidity, shame, dissimulation, and fickleness — inferred from the agitation, turning the face, covering the cheeks, and embracing her friend. This is <s>niṣpatti</s> (fruition) of rasa in the form of <s>rati</s>.
Through the excellence of the object, locus, cultivation, qualities, nature, and skill,
and through the superabundance of excitation — the intensification (of <s>rasa</s>) is desired as <s>puṣṭi</s> (nourishment). // Ckc_5.19 //
For example:

children.text: avyājaspṛhaṇīyamañcati parāṃ kāntiṃ sakhīnāṃ puraḥ śrīsiṅgakṣitināyakena sutanoraṅgaṃ samāliṅgatam /
children.translated_text: Embraced by King <s>Śrī Siṅga</s>, the earth's lord, the body of the beautiful one attains supreme loveliness, genuinely desirable, before her friends;

children.text: svājñānirvahaṇena nirvṛtamanāstatkālamīladdṛśe yasmai puṣpaśarāsanaḥ svasukṛtaiḥ kalyāṇamāśaṃsate // Ckc_5.*9 //
children.translated_text: at that moment, the god of flowery bow (<s>Kāma</s>), his mind satisfied by the carrying out of his own command, with half-closed eyes, wishes auspiciousness upon him through his own good merits. // Ckc_5.*9 //

children.text: atra rūpayauvanaviśeṣaśīlādiguṇasaṃpannāṃ nāyikāmuddiśya samutpannā dhīralalitaprakṛte rāśrayabhūtasya nāyakasya ratiḥ paricayopacitena saṃskārapāṭavena paribodhyamānā svabhāvasundaratadaṅga sanniveśarāmaṇīyakavibhāvanoddīpanātiśayena dīpyamānā sakhīnāṃ samakṣamanyāliṅganalakṣaṇaśarīrāraṃbhānubhāvānumīyamānāṃ lajjātyāgalakṣaṇāṃ saptamīṃ rasāvasthāmadhyāste /
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>rati</s> of the hero — of gentle and playful nature — directed toward the heroine endowed with special beauty, youth, character, and other qualities, being awakened by the skill of cultivated familiarity, being kindled by the superabundance of excitation through the naturally beautiful arrangement of her limbs, and inferred through the bodily consequent of embracing her before her friends — reaches the seventh stage of <s>rasa</s>, characterized by the abandonment of shame.

children.text: kiñca samagrātmaguṇa saṃpadā nāyakamuddiśya samutpannā sthirānurāgasarasaprakṛteḥ nāyikāyā ratiḥ paricayānukūlyābyāmutkaṭena vāsanā pāṭavena prabodhyamānā prakṛṣṭapremapriyatamāliṅganadīpanātiśayenoddīpyamānāṃ nayananimīlanānubhāvānumīyamānāṃ navamīṃ premapuṣṭimavasthā madhitiṣṭhatīti seyaṃ rasapuṣṭiḥ //
children.translated_text: Furthermore, the <s>rati</s> of the heroine — of steadfast, passionate nature — directed toward the hero endowed with the fullness of all personal virtues, being awakened by the intense skill of impressions favorable to familiarity, and being kindled by the superabundance of excitation through the beloved's embrace of supreme love, and inferred through the consequent of closing the eyes — reaches the ninth stage, the <s>premapuṣṭi</s> (nourishment of love). This is <s>rasapuṣṭi</s> (nourishment of rasa).
The tenfold stages of <s>premapuṣṭi</s> (love's nourishment) have been illustrated in the <s>Siṅgabhūpālīya</s>. // Ckc_5.20 //
<s>Abhilāṣa</s> (longing), <s>cintana</s> (thinking), <s>anusmṛti</s> (recollection), <s>guṇasaṃkīrtana</s> (praising qualities), <s>udvega</s> (agitation),

children.text: savilāsā unmādavyādhī jaḍatā mṛtiśca daśadhā tāḥ // Ckc_5.21 //
children.translated_text: <s>vilāsa</s> (coquetry), <s>unmāda</s> (madness), <s>vyādhi</s> (sickness), <s>jaḍatā</s> (stupor), and <s>mṛti</s> (death) — these are the ten stages. // Ckc_5.21 //

children.text:
kramaśo darśayati /
nanu tatra pūrvānurāgākhyavipralaṃbhajanyatayā tadidaṃ daśādaśakaṃ (pradarśakaṃ) pradarśitam /
atra tu saṃbhogena kathaṃ nirūpyata iti ceducyate /
vipralaṃbhe prāyeṇa kavibhiretadāpoṣitamityabhiprāyeṇa /
na tu saṃbhoge tanniṣedhāyeti veditavyam /
children.translated_text: They are shown in order. Now, there, these ten stages have been illustrated as arising from <s>vipralambha</s> (love-in-separation) named <s>pūrvānurāga</s> (prior love). But here, how can they be demonstrated in <s>saṃbhoga</s> (love-in-union)? The answer: because poets have generally nourished these in <s>vipralambha</s>; but this does not mean they are prohibited in <s>saṃbhoga</s> — this should be understood.
When there is another emotion of equal strength arising simultaneously,

children.text: yastena tasya saṃsargaḥ sa saṅkara itīritaḥ // Ckc_5.22 //
children.translated_text: and there is a mingling of that with the other — that is called <s>saṅkara</s> (mixture). // Ckc_5.22 //
For example:
At every sight of King <s>Siṅga</s>, her beloved who had previously offended,
the proud woman drowns in the waves of wonder, anger, and affection. // Ckc_5.*10 //

children.text: atra vismayaroṣasnehā yathocitaṃ tatpūrvāparādhatayā dṛṣṭatayā vallabhatayā bhaktijanitāstattadāśritaviśeṣavibhāvanoddīpyamānāḥ paramaparipoṣalakṣaṇakathāsvabhāvavāckaśabdaprayogaśaktyā yathocitaṃ sūcitairanimeṣādharasphuraṇanīvībandhavisraṃsanādibhiranubhāvaiḥ stambhavaivarṇyaromāñcādibhissācvikairanuvaddhā ūrmipadadyotitairvitartaharṣādivyabhicāribhi staraṅgitāstulyakālabalotpattihetutayā saṃkīrṇāśca rasasaṅkarapratītimaṅkurayantīti rasasaṅkaroktiriyam /
children.translated_text: Here, wonder, anger, and affection — generated respectively by his offense, by seeing him, and by his being her beloved — each kindled by its appropriate particular <s>vibhāva</s> (determinant), indicated through appropriate consequents such as unblinking gaze, trembling lip, and loosening of the girdle-knot (inferred through <s>sāttvika</s> responses of stupefaction, pallor, and horripilation), stirred by transient emotions of deliberation and joy (conveyed by the word 'wave') — these, being of equal temporal and causal strength, produce the perception of <s>rasasaṅkara</s> (mixture of rasas). This is a statement of <s>rasasaṅkara</s>.

children.text: ārūḍhasya parāṃ kāṣṭhāṃ yena kenāpi hetunā /
children.translated_text: The decline of a <s>rasa</s> that has risen to its highest peak,

children.text: rasasyāpacayo yasya taṃ hrāsaṃ kavayo viduḥ // Ckc_5.23 //
children.translated_text: due to whatever cause — that the poets know as <s>hrāsa</s> (diminution). // Ckc_5.23 //
For example:

children.text: śvāso yena yayā ca bhāṣaṇavidhau vyālokane pakṣmaṇāṃ vyāpāraḥ pariraṃbhaṇe malayajaṃ pratyūha ityūhyate /
children.translated_text: His breathing — through which the mode of speech was (affected) — and the function of eyelashes in gazing, and sandal-paste in embracing — these are thought to be obstacles;

children.text: tāmāpṛcchati rājaśailagataye pāṇṅyassa tasmai ca sā sevārītimupādiśantyanusamācāreṇa cakre natim // Ckc_5.*11 //
children.translated_text: she bids him farewell for his journey to the royal mountain; and he, presenting his hand (in parting), and she, instructing him on the protocol of service, bowed according to custom. // Ckc_5.*11 //

children.text:
atra prativirodhināṃ niḥśvāsādīnāṃ bhāṣaṇādisaṃbhogapratyūhatvābhimānalakṣaṇena cittārambhānubhāvena kṛtapratīterudvegalakṣaṇāyāḥ pāṇḍyatadavarodhayoḥ premapuṣṭerapacayo rājyadhvaṃsavanavāsādiparikleśa hetuko bhavati /
ekatra nāyakasevārthaṃ rājagirigamanāyāmantraṇena vāgārambhaṇenānyatra sevāprakāropadeśasamācāranatibhyāṃ vākkāyasaṃraṃbhānubhāvābhyāṃ pratīyata iti seyaṃ rasahrāsoktiḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>premapuṣṭi</s> (nourishment of love) of the <s>Pāṇḍya</s> king and his queen — whose intensity was established through the mental consequent of considering even sighing, blinking, and such as obstacles to speech, gazing, and embracing — undergoes decline due to the distress of the destruction of the kingdom and forest-exile. On the one hand, through the verbal consequent of summoning for departure to the royal mountain for the hero's service, and on the other, through the verbal and bodily consequents of instructing on the mode of service and bowing in custom — this is the statement of <s>rasahrāsa</s> (diminution of rasa).
When, due to the impropriety of the <s>ālambana</s> (object), a rasa that even manifests clearly
is somewhat laughed at — this is called <s>ābhāsa</s> (semblance of rasa). // Ckc_5.24 //

children.text:
tatra śṛṅgārābhāsaścaturdhā īritaḥ /
ekatra rāgasyābhāvādanekatra vaiṣamyeṇa saṃbhavāttiryagālaṃbanatvānmlecchālaṃbanatvācca /
atra rāgāsaṃbhavastridhā--prāgabhāvāt, pradhvaṃsābhāvādatyantābhāvācca /
atra rāgaprāgabhāvaviṣaye nābhāsatā /
darśanādisāmagrīsaṃbhave rāgotpatteḥ saṃbhāvyamānatvāditarayostvābhāsataiva /
children.translated_text: There, <s>śṛṅgārābhāsa</s> (semblance of erotic sentiment) is stated to be fourfold: due to the absence of passion in one party, due to inequality in multiple parties, due to an animal being the <s>ālambana</s> (object), and due to a <s>mleccha</s> (barbarian) being the <s>ālambana</s>. Here, the impossibility of passion is threefold — due to prior non-existence, due to subsequent destruction, and due to absolute absence. Regarding the prior non-existence of passion, there is no semblance, since the arising of passion is possible when the aggregate of conditions such as seeing etc. is present; but in the other two cases, there is indeed semblance.
An example of the absolute absence of passion:

children.text: vyarthatvaṃ gamitā kaṭākṣasaraṇiḥ sākūtamandasmitā vyaṅgyoktirvitathā vṛthā viracitastādṛk praṇāmāñjaliḥ /
children.translated_text: The path of sidelong glances has been rendered futile, the suggestive gentle smile made pointless, the implied speech false, and such a reverential salutation with folded hands made in vain —

children.text: necchatyanyaparigrahaṃ kila vadhūṃ recarlavaṃśāgraṇīḥ sakhyastvaṃ ca suhurmuhuḥ smarata māṃ so 'yaṃ hi satyavrataḥ // Ckc_5.*12 //
children.translated_text: For the chief of the <s>Recarla</s> lineage does not desire another man's wife, they say. O friend, you too should remember me again and again — for he is indeed a man of truthful vows.

children.text:
atra muhurmahurātmasmaraṇa prārthanālakṣaṇāṃ sakhījanāmantraṇavāgāraṃbhānubhāvānumitāṃ tanutyāgodyogalakṣaṇāṃ parāṃ puṣṭimadhitiṣṭhan parakīyāyāḥ nāyikāyā anurāgo viṣayabhūte nāyakaratne parastrī viṣayarāgātyantābhāvādekataḥ khaṇḍito 'pi śṛṅgāramivābhāsayatīti so 'yaṃ rasābhāsoktiḥ /
evamanyadapyudāhāryam /
children.translated_text: Here, the passion of the <s>parakīyā</s> (another's wife) <s>nāyikā</s> (heroine) — which attains the highest intensity characterized by readiness to abandon her body, inferred through the <s>anubhāva</s> (consequent) of initiating speech addressing her female companions, marked by the entreaty that he remember her again and again — produces a semblance as if it were <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment), though it is truncated on one side, because in the hero who is the object there is an absolute absence of passion toward another's wife. Thus this is called an expression of <s>rasābhāsa</s> (semblance of rasa). Other examples too may be similarly cited.
When powerful opposing causes arise,
The complete closing down of the abundance of <s>rasa</s> from its very root is called <s>śama</s> (quieting).
For example:

children.text: siṅgakṣoṇibhujaḥ kaliṅgakubhuje kruddhasya tasmin kṣaṇe dattāṃ tattanayāmupāyanatayā lokottamāṃ paśyataḥ /
children.translated_text: When the lord of <s>Siṅga</s>, angered at the king of <s>Kaliṅga</s>, at that very moment beholds his extraordinary daughter offered as a gift —

children.text: vyāvṛttā dhanuṣaḥ kaṭākṣasaraṇistadbhrūlatālokinī dṛkkoṇaṃ parihṛtya rāgamahimā cite paraṃ ceṣṭate // Ckc_5.*13 //
children.translated_text: The path of sidelong glances turns away from the bow, gazing upon the creeper of her brow; abandoning the corner of the eye directed at him, the majesty of passion acts supremely upon the heart.

children.text: atra pūrvamārūḍho 'pi kaliṅganarapālagocaro nāyakasya krodho balavatā samucitopāyanasamarpaṇajanitaprasādopabṛhitena kaliṅgarājakanyakāgocareṇa premṇā niravaśeṣamupaśāmyata iti seyaṃ rasaśamoktiḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, the hero's anger directed at the king of <s>Kaliṅga</s>, though it had already arisen, is completely quieted by love directed at the princess of <s>Kaliṅga</s>, nourished by the grace born of the offering of a fitting gift. Thus this is an expression of <s>rasaśama</s> (quieting of rasa).
Due to the stability of latent impressions of a <s>rasa</s>, or due to gentle disposition,

children.text: pralīnasyāpi yo gandhaḥ sa śeṣa iti gīyate // Ckc_5.26 //
children.translated_text: The lingering fragrance of a <s>rasa</s> even after it has dissolved is celebrated as <s>śeṣa</s> (residue).
For example:

children.text: śyāmāyāḥ kucamaṇḍale na parayorṇattebhakumbhadvaye dṛṣṭiṃ rāgataraṅgitāṃ vidadhatā śrīsiṅgabhūmībhujā /
children.translated_text: While the lord of <s>Siṅga</s> directs his gaze, trembling with waves of passion, not upon the breast-region of the dark-complexioned beloved nor upon the pot-like frontal globes of the other two rival women —

children.text: dākṣiṇyavratabhhagabhīrumanasā devena vāmabhruvā- manyāsāmapi sā tathaiva kṛtinā netrakriyā nāpyasau // Ckc_5.*14 //
children.translated_text: That skillful lord, with a mind fearful of breaking his vow of courtesy toward the left-browed women, bestows the same glance upon those others too — yet that act of the eyes is not the same.

children.text:
atra dhīralalitaprakṛternāyakasya śyāmāgocareṇa balavatā premṇā pralīnatāmānītasyāpi taditaranāyikāgocarasya premṇo viśeṣaḥ kaṭākṣapradāna dākṣiṇyena pratibhātata iti seyaṃ rasaśeṣoktiḥ /
evaṃ hāsyādiṣvapi raseṣu sphurattādi daśoktiprakārāḥ svayamanusandheyāḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, the love of the hero — who is of the <s>dhīralalita</s> (gentle-refined) type — directed toward the dark-complexioned woman, though it has brought even his love for the other heroines to a state of dissolution through its intensity, is nonetheless perceived through the special courtesy of bestowing sidelong glances upon them. Thus this is an expression of <s>rasaśeṣa</s> (residue of rasa). Similarly, in <s>hāsya</s> (comic) and other <s>rasas</s> too, the ten types of expression such as <s>sphurattā</s> (manifestation) etc. should be investigated by the reader on their own.
Our particular interest lies in the elaboration of <s>alaṅkāra</s> (figures of speech);
Nevertheless, we briefly state the delineation of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> and other <s>rasas</s>.

children.text: atra śṛṅgāro nāma caturastrīpuṃsālaṃbano manoharapadārthoddīpano lalitabhrūlatāvikṣepakaṭākṣamandasmitādyanubhāvo nikhilasācvikotsukatvogratā lasyajugupsāvahitthādipariśiṣṭa sañcāripuṣṭo ratisthāyībhāvo vipralaṃbhasaṃbhogabhedavān vigalita vedyāntaratvalakṣaṇaṃ cetovikāsamadhitiṣṭhati /
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>rasa</s> called <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment) has as its <s>ālambana</s> (object) an accomplished man and woman, as its <s>uddīpana</s> (stimulus) charming objects, as its <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequents) graceful movements of the brow-creeper, sidelong glances, gentle smiles and the like, is enriched by all <s>sāttvika</s> (psychophysical) responses, and by <s>sañcārin</s> (transitory) emotions — eagerness, intensity, langour, disgust, dissimulation and the rest — and has <s>rati</s> (love) as its <s>sthāyībhāva</s> (permanent emotion). It is of two kinds, <s>vipralambha</s> (love in separation) and <s>saṃbhoga</s> (love in union), and manifests the state of mental blossoming characterized by the dissolution of awareness of anything else.
An example of <s>vipralambha</s> (love in separation):
By the moonlight, sandalwood-scented breezes, which greatly agitate her heart, at the time of separation from the lord of <s>Siṅga</s>, upon whom her longing has mounted in full splendor —

children.text: niḥśvāsaglapitādharaṃ paritatassaṃruddhavāṣpodayaṃ tanvyā snigdhasakhījane viracitā dīnā dṛśorvṛttayaḥ // Ckc_5.*15 //
children.translated_text: The slender woman directs toward her affectionate circle of friends pitiful movements of her eyes, with lips withered by sighs, and tears welling up on all sides restrained.

children.text: atra nāyakagocarā kasyāśvinnāyikāyā ratirabhīṣṭāliṅganādyaprāptāvapi prakṛṣyamāṇā candracandanamārūtai śvakārādanuktasamuccitaiḥ puṃskokilālāpibhi ssamuddīpyamānā niḥśvāsādiśarīrāraṃbhānubhāvai ssūcitā bāṣpādisācvikaiḥ prakāśitā tanutvadīnadṛṣṭyādyānumitaiḥ glāniśramaviṣādāvegadainyādisañjāribhirabhipoṣitā vigalitavedyāntaratayā bhāvakacetasi vikāso pādhikā sphurantī śṛṅgārarasatāmāpadyata iti so 'yaṃ tathoktaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>rati</s> (love) of a certain <s>nāyikā</s> directed toward the hero, though the desired embrace and such have not been attained, is intensified and stimulated by the moon, sandalwood-paste, breezes, and unstated additional factors included by the word 'and' such as the songs of male cuckoos; it is indicated by bodily <s>anubhāvas</s> such as sighing, revealed by <s>sāttvika</s> responses such as tears, nourished by <s>sañcārin</s> (transitory) emotions such as weariness, fatigue, despondency, agitation, and wretchedness — inferred from her emaciation, pitiful gaze and the like — and, with the dissolution of awareness of anything else, it shines forth as productive of blossoming in the heart of the sensitive spectator, thus attaining the state of <s>śṛṅgāra rasa</s>. Therefore it is so designated.
An example of <s>saṃbhoga śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment of union):

children.text: avyājaspṛhaṇīyamañcati parāṃ kāntiṃ sakhīnāṃ puraḥ śrīsiṅgabhitināyakena sutanoraṅgaṃ samāliṅgitam /
children.translated_text: Displaying an unaffectedly enviable supreme radiance before her friends, the slender woman's body is embraced by the hero, the lord of <s>Siṅga</s> —

children.text: svājñānirvahaṇena nirvṛtamanāstatkālamīladdṛśe yasmai puṣpaśarāsanaḥ svasukṛtaiḥ kalyāṇamāśaṃsate // Ckc_5.*16 //
children.translated_text: Content in mind through the fulfillment of her own wishes, with eyes closed at that moment, to whom <s>Puṣpaśarāsana</s> (the Flower-Arrowed One, i.e., <s>Kāmadeva</s>) himself, by his own merits, wishes auspiciousness.

children.text: hāsyo nāma kubjavāmanādisamalambanastatsvarūpādibhāvanoddīpano nayanavistāragaṇḍamaṇḍala vikāsasvandhanikuñcanādyanubhāvo bāṣpasvedādisācviko harṣāvahitthādhṛtipramukhasañjārīhāsyasthāyībhāvaḥ smitavihasitādi bhedavān vikāsopādhireva vilasati /
children.translated_text: The <s>rasa</s> called <s>hāsya</s> (comic sentiment) has as its <s>ālambana</s> (object) hunchbacks, dwarfs and the like, as its <s>uddīpana</s> (stimulus) the contemplation of their peculiar forms and such, as its <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequents) widening of the eyes, blooming of the cheeks, contraction of the nose and the like, as its <s>sāttvika</s> responses tears and perspiration and such, is enriched by <s>sañcārin</s> (transitory) emotions such as joy, dissimulation, and composure, and has <s>hāsa</s> (laughter) as its <s>sthāyībhāva</s> (permanent emotion). It is of varieties such as <s>smita</s> (smile), <s>vihasita</s> (laughter) and so on, and shines forth as having the very condition of blossoming as its defining attribute.
For example:

children.text: strīpuṃsau gaḍurāvupāyanakṛtau dvīpāntarādhīśvarair īkṣitvā vikasatkapolamadhipo līlābjamājighrati /
children.translated_text: Seeing a pair of hunchbacks, male and female, presented as gifts by rulers of island-kingdoms, the king smells his sport-lotus with cheeks blossoming wide,

children.text: rājādressacivā hasanti vikasannetraṃ vibhugvāṃsakaṃ saṃpīḍyāpahasanti pārśvayugalīṃ bāṣpāvilākṣaṃ janāḥ // Ckc_5.*17 //
children.translated_text: The ministers of the royal court laugh with eyes wide open; the lord, pressing his shoulder, suppresses his laughter; the attendants on both sides shed tears with eyes brimming.

children.text:
atra kubjamithunaviṣayo nāyakādisamāśraya hāsaḥ tadīyastrīpuṃsavyāpārābhāsabhāvanoddīpitaḥ kapolavikāsādinā śarīrāraṃbhānubhāvena sūcito līlāravindasamāghrāṇādyanumitenāvahitthālakṣaṇasañcāriṇā paripuṣṭo manovikāsamadhitiṣṭhatīti so 'yaṃ hāsyaḥ /
vīro nāma prakṛṣṭaprakṛtināyakāśrayo lokottaravastuviṣayastādṛśapurāvṛttapuruṣakārānubandhāsaha sahajasacvādisamuddīpanavibhāvo mukhaprasādavāhusphuraṇakṛpāṇanirīkṣaṇapramukhānubhāvo romāñcavepathuprabhṛtisācviko harṣāsūyāmarṣamatidhṛtipramukhasañcāribhāvakalpitaśrīrutsāhasthāyībhāvaścetaso vistāramadhitiṣṭhati /
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>hāsa</s> (laughter) directed at the hunchback couple, residing in the king and others, is stimulated by the contemplation of the semblance of the man-woman interaction of that pair, indicated by the bodily <s>anubhāva</s> of the blooming of the cheeks and such, and nourished by the <s>sañcārin</s> (transitory) emotion characterized as <s>avahitthā</s> (dissimulation) — inferred from the smelling of the sport-lotus and such — and thus it manifests as mental blossoming. This is <s>hāsya</s> (the comic sentiment). The <s>rasa</s> called <s>vīra</s> (heroic sentiment) resides in a hero of superior nature, has as its object extraordinary things, has as its <s>vibhāvas</s> the stimulation of innate valor and similar qualities through association with past exploits of great men, has as its <s>anubhāvas</s> radiance of face, flexing of arms, gazing at the sword and such, has <s>sāttvika</s> responses such as horripilation and trembling, is adorned by <s>sañcārin</s> (transitory) emotions such as joy, envy, indignation, resolve and composure, and has <s>utsāha</s> (enthusiasm) as its <s>sthāyībhāva</s> (permanent emotion), and manifests as expansion of the heart.
For example:

children.text: rāmasya śrutasindhubandhanavidhiḥ bāhū nijau vīkṣate prītiṃ naiti digantarājavijaye dvīpāntarāṇāṃ śruteḥ /
children.translated_text: Having heard of <s>Rāma</s>'s feat of bridging the ocean, he gazes at his own two arms; he takes no delight upon hearing of the conquest of kings of distant regions and island-kingdoms;

children.text: na ślāghāṃ bahumanyate vitaraṇe deveṣvasaṃprārthiṣu śrīsiṅgakṣitināthamaṇḍanamaṇī recarlavaṃśāgraṇīḥ // Ckc_5.*18 //
children.translated_text: He does not regard praise highly when giving to gods who have not even asked — such is the crest-jewel adorning the lord of <s>Siṅga</s>, the chief of the <s>Recarla</s> lineage.

children.text:
atra nāyakottamāśrayo lokottaratvaprāptiviṣaya utsāho rāmabhadrāpadāna śravaṇādinoddīpito rājabāhunirīkṣaṇalakṣitarāmabhadraviṣayaspardhāviśeṣāt jambūdvīparājaviṣayānādarācca prakāśitenādhikaspadāṃ nivārayeti lakṣaṇavatā śobhānāmnā pauruṣasācvikena dvīpāntarajayāśaṃsālakṣaṇena cittāraṃbhānubhāvena cābhivyakto 'sūyādhṛtimatigarvādibhirupacito manovistāramadhitiṣṭhatīti so 'yaṃ yuddhavīraḥ /
tathā ca tatraiva dānavīro 'pi devatākartṛkārthitvākāṅakṣālakṣaṇena cittārambhānubhāvenābhivyakto devatālabhyavastuviśeṣavitaraṇakaṇḍūlatālakṣaṇaṃ paramotkarṣamārohati /
adbhutanāmā lokottaradarśanādivibhāvo nayananaiśvalyaśirodhūnanachoṭikāsādhuvādādyanubhāvaḥ pulakādisācviko harṣacāpalya dhṛtimatipramukhasañcāribhāvo vismayasthāyībāvaśvittavistāramevādhitiṣṭhati /
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>utsāha</s> (enthusiasm) residing in the supreme hero and directed toward the attainment of extraordinary glory is stimulated by hearing of the exploits of <s>Rāmabhadra</s> and such, and is manifested through the rivalry toward <s>Rāmabhadra</s> marked by the hero's gazing at his own royal arms, and through the disdain for the conquest of the kings of <s>Jambudvīpa</s>, by the <s>sāttvika</s> response called <s>śobhā</s> (splendor) characterized as 'preventing anything from being a greater arena,' and by the psychic <s>anubhāva</s> characterized as the expectation of conquering island-kingdoms; it is amplified by envy, composure, resolve, pride and the like, and manifests as expansion of the mind. Thus this is <s>yuddha-vīra</s> (the heroic sentiment of battle). Likewise, in the same passage, the <s>dāna-vīra</s> (heroic sentiment of generosity) too is manifested through the psychic <s>anubhāva</s> characterized by the absence of desire on the part of the divine recipients, and ascends to supreme excellence characterized as the eagerness to give extraordinary things attainable only by the gods. The <s>rasa</s> called <s>adbhuta</s> (wondrous sentiment) has as its <s>vibhāva</s> the sight of extraordinary things and such, has as its <s>anubhāvas</s> fixity of the eyes, shaking of the head, snapping of the fingers, exclamations of 'well done!' and the like, has <s>sāttvika</s> responses such as horripilation, is enriched by <s>sañcārin</s> emotions such as joy, restlessness, composure and resolve, and has <s>vismaya</s> (wonder) as its <s>sthāyībhāva</s>, and manifests precisely as expansion of the heart.
For example:

children.text: śrutvā saṃsadi siṅgabhūpacaritaṃ dattaṃ havistadadvijair ādātuṃ bhuvamāgataiḥ pratigatairākhyātamindrādibhiḥ /
children.translated_text: Having heard in the assembly the exploits of the king of <s>Siṅga</s>, <s>Dilīpa</s> and the other ancient kings — to whom oblations were offered by Brahmins who had come to earth to receive them, and whose deeds were recounted by <s>Indra</s> and other gods upon their return —

children.text: anyonyaṃ kila sādhusādhviti kṛtālāpā dilīpādayaḥ prāntasphāravilokitā pulakitā mūrdhānamādhunvate // Ckc_5.*19 //
children.translated_text: Speaking to one another 'well done, well done!' indeed, with gazes sweeping wide to the edges, bristling with horripilation, they shake their heads in wonder.

children.text:
atra kalikālo 'pi dharṇapratiṣṭhāpanādināyakapuṇyacaritaviṣayo dilīpādipurātanamahārājasamāśrayo vismayo mahendrādisamādaraṇodāharaṇābhyāmuddīpito nayanastaimityā dyanubhāvānumitaḥ pulakasācvikena viśeṣataḥ prakāśitaḥ sādhuvādaśiraḥ kampānumitairharṣacāpalādibhirabhipuṣṭaśvittavistāralakṣaṇamupādhimupāt iṣṭhata iti so 'yamadbhutarasaḥ /
raudro nāma krūrajanasamāśrayo /
aparādhiviṣayaḥ tadapakārasmaraṇapramukoddīpano bhrūbhaṅgadantaghaṭṭanarūkṣekṣaṇādyanubhāvaḥ svedavepathupramukhasācviko 'marṣābhyasūyā cāpalogratādisañcāribhāvaprapañcitaḥ krodhasthāyībhāvaḥ cittavikṣobhalakṣaṇamupādhimanusaṃdhatte /
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>vismaya</s> (wonder) directed at the meritorious deeds of the hero — who even in the <s>Kali</s> age performs acts such as the establishment of <s>dharma</s> — resides in the ancient great kings such as <s>Dilīpa</s> and others, is stimulated by the examples of honor shown by great <s>Indra</s> and others, is inferred from <s>anubhāvas</s> such as fixity of the eyes, is especially revealed by the <s>sāttvika</s> response of horripilation, is nourished by joy, restlessness and the like — inferred from exclamations of 'well done!' and the shaking of heads — and manifests the condition characterized as expansion of the heart. Thus this is <s>adbhuta rasa</s> (the wondrous sentiment). The <s>rasa</s> named <s>raudra</s> (terrible sentiment) resides in cruel persons, has as its object offenders, is stimulated by the remembrance of their offenses and such, has as its <s>anubhāvas</s> contraction of the brows, gnashing of teeth, harsh glances and the like, has <s>sāttvika</s> responses such as perspiration and trembling, is elaborated by <s>sañcārin</s> (transitory) emotions such as indignation, envy, fickleness, and ferocity, and has <s>krodha</s> (anger) as its <s>sthāyībhāva</s> (permanent emotion), and assumes the condition characterized as agitation of the mind.
For example:
With sparks of the fire of wrath scattering and flashing at every cast of the eyes, terrifying with the eruption of furrowed brows, harshly roaring with lips bitten by gnashing teeth,

children.text: durvārākharvagarvajvarabharaghaṭita svedamādhūtagātraṃ bhinte śrīsiṅgabhūpapratibhaṭapaṭalaṃ niṣkṛpaste kṛpāṇaḥ // Ckc_5.*20 //
children.translated_text: With body drenched in sweat produced by the weight of the fever of irresistible, undiminished pride, shaking violently — the merciless sword of the lord of <s>Siṅga</s> cleaves through the ranks of his adversaries.

children.text:
atra pratibhaṭasamāśrayo nāyakagocaraḥ krodhasthāyī deśākramaṇabandhuvadhabandhanādibhiruddīpyamāno bhrūbhaṅgadantakarṣaṇauṣṭha saṃdaṃśanādibhirabhilakṣitaḥ svedavepathubhyāṃ sāttvikābhyāṃ prakāśamānastadupalakṣitaireva garvāmarṣacāpalogratāmarṣādibhirvyabhicāribhiḥ puṣṭo bhāvakānāṃ cetasi vikṣobhalakṣaṇāmānandalaharīmunmudrayan raudra ityākhyāyate /
karuṇo nāma vipannasuhṛdādiviṣayaḥ tadguṇasmaraṇādyuddīpano vilāpapatanādyanubhāvo vaivarṇyastambhāśrumukhasāttviko nirvedaglāniviṣādadainyāvegonmādādisañcārī śokasthāyībhāvo manovikṣobhalakṣaṇamevopādhimanusandhatte /
children.translated_text: Here, the <s>sthāyībhāva</s> of <s>krodha</s> (anger) directed at the adversaries and residing in the hero, stimulated by invasion of his territory, slaughter of kinsmen, imprisonment and such, marked by the contraction of brows, grinding of teeth, biting of lips and the like, revealed by the <s>sāttvika</s> responses of perspiration and trembling, and nourished by <s>vyabhicārin</s> (transitory) emotions such as pride, indignation, fickleness, ferocity, and fury — which are indicated by those very signs — is called <s>raudra</s> (the terrible sentiment), as it unfolds in the hearts of the sensitive spectators a wave of bliss characterized as agitation. The <s>rasa</s> named <s>karuṇa</s> (pathetic sentiment) has as its object afflicted friends and the like, is stimulated by the remembrance of their virtues and such, has as its <s>anubhāvas</s> lamentation, falling down and the like, has <s>sāttvika</s> responses of pallor, stupefaction, tears and such, has <s>sañcārin</s> (transitory) emotions of world-weariness, languor, despondency, wretchedness, agitation, madness and the like, and has <s>śoka</s> (grief) as its <s>sthāyībhāva</s>, and assumes the very condition characterized as agitation of the mind.
For example:

children.text: etattadvadanaṃ kimeṣa sabhujaḥ se 'yaṃ tavorassthalī hā prāṇeśa halāsmi nāsmi dalitā gāḍhaṃ khalu strīmanaḥ /
children.translated_text: Is this that very face? Is this the same one with those arms? Is this your chest? Alas, O lord of my life! I am undone, I am no more! Truly, a woman's heart is crushed utterly —

children.text: ityādīni raṇāṅgaṇeṣu gaṇaśaḥ śrīsiṅgabhūpadviṣa- ddevīnāṃ paridevitāni karuṇāṃ śraṇvanti bhūtānyapi // Ckc_5.*21 //
children.translated_text: Such and similar lamentations of the queens of the enemies of the lord of <s>Siṅga</s>, uttered in droves upon the battlefields — even the ghosts listen to them with compassion.

children.text:
atra nāyakaśatrukulabālikāśrayo vipannavallabhaviṣayaḥ śokasthāyī khaṇḍīkṛtaḥ tatastato viparyastatadavayavapratyabhijñādibhiruddīpyamānaḥ tadetaditivāgārambhamavyabhicaratā nirdeśalakṣaṇena hastārambhānubhāvena sūcitaḥ tadanusaraṇapariṇatiravaśyaṃ bhāvināśrupātavaivarṇyādinā sāttvikasamudayena prakāśitaḥ tattaducitahāprāṇeśādivāgārambhānumitairdainyaviṣādanirvedamatibhiḥvyabhicār ibhirādipadadyotita paridevitaviśeṣopakalpitaiḥ glāniśramaśaṅgācāpalonmādādibhiranyaiśva paripoṣito nīrasatayā sthāṇuprāyāṇāmapi bhūtabetālātmakādīnāma pyanukampātiśayasampādakatayā bhāvukacetasi vikṣobhapuṣṭi madhitiṣṭhan karuṇa ityākhyāyate /
bībhatso nāma heyavastuviṣayaḥ taddoṣadarśanādibhiruddīpito nāsāgrapidhānamukhakūṇananetrasaṃkocanā dyanubhāvo vaivarṇyādisāttviko nirvedāvegacāpalavrīḍādivyabhicārī jugupsāsthāyībhāvo vidagdhabhāvakacetasi vikṣepalakṣaṇāmānandabhūmikāmālaṃbate /
children.translated_text: Here, the permanent emotion (<s>sthāyibhāva</s>) of grief (<s>śoka</s>), whose object is the ruined beloved and whose locus is the young women of the hero's enemy's family, is fragmented; then it is enflamed here and there by the recognition of the scattered parts (of the beloved's remnants) and the like. It is indicated by the involuntary sign (<s>anubhāva</s>) of raising the hand (in gestures), characterized by pointing — with verbal beginnings like 'this is that' — and by unerring designation. Its culmination in that pursuit is necessarily manifested by the confluence of <s>sāttvika</s> (psychophysical) reactions such as tears, pallor, and the like, which are bound to occur. It is nourished by transitory emotions (<s>vyabhicārin</s>) such as dejection (<s>dainya</s>), despondency (<s>viṣāda</s>), world-weariness (<s>nirveda</s>), and confusion (<s>mati</s>), inferred from the appropriate verbal beginnings like 'Alas! O lord of my life!' and the like, enhanced by particular forms of lamentation, and by others such as languor (<s>glāni</s>), fatigue (<s>śrama</s>), apprehension (<s>śaṅkā</s>), agitation (<s>cāpala</s>), madness (<s>unmāda</s>), and the like. Because even beings as inert as tree-trunks, including ghosts and vampires (<s>bhūta-betāla</s>), produce an abundance of compassion due to (their) very lifelessness — (this rasa), persisting in the form of agitation enriched in the heart of the sensitive connoisseur (<s>bhāvuka</s>), is called <s>karuṇa</s> (the compassionate rasa). The <s>bībhatsa</s> (disgusting rasa) has repulsive objects as its subject; it is enflamed by the perception of their faults and the like; its involuntary signs are covering the tip of the nose, grimacing, contracting the eyes, and the like; its <s>sāttvika</s> reactions are pallor and the like; its transitory emotions are world-weariness, agitation, fickleness, shame, and the like; and the permanent emotion is disgust (<s>jugupsā</s>) — it rests upon the plane of bliss characterized by agitation in the heart of the refined connoisseur.
For example —

children.text: aṃhaśśeṣairiva parivṛto makṣikāmaṇḍalībhiḥ pūyaklinnaṃ vraṇamabhimṛśan vāsasaḥ khaṇḍakena /
children.translated_text: Surrounded by swarms of flies as if by remnants of sin, touching the pus-soaked wound with a scrap of cloth,

children.text: rathyāprānte drutamapasṛtaṃ saṃkucannetrakoṇaṃ channaghrāṇaṃ racayati janaṃ dadrurogī daridraḥ // Ckc_5.*22 //
children.translated_text: the poor man afflicted with ringworm, on the roadside, causes people to quickly retreat, contracting the corners of their eyes, covering their noses. // Ckc_5.*22 //

children.text:
atra nāyakaśatrudadrurogiviṣayā janāśrayā jugupsā vraṇāmarśanā dibhiruddīpitā netrasaṃkocanādibhirabhivyaktā parāpasaraṇānumitairāvegacāpalādibhiḥpoṣitā bhāvaka cetasi vikṣepalakṣaṇamupādhimādadhānā bībhatsa ityākhyāyate /
bhayānako nāma bhīṣaṇavastuviṣayo mukhaśoṣatālupuṭalehananīcairgamanādyanubhāvo, aśruvarjita sāttviko viṣādaśaṅkātrāsāvegadainyajaḍatā glāniśramacintāpasmārādisaṃcāribhāvo bhayasthāyībhāvaścittavikṣepalakṣaṇāmeva bhūmikāmālambate /
children.translated_text: Here, the disgust (<s>jugupsā</s>), whose object is the hero's enemy suffering from ringworm and whose locus is the people, is enflamed by the touching of the wound and the like, manifested by the contraction of the eyes and the like, nourished by agitation and fickleness inferred from the retreat of others — imposing upon the connoisseur's heart the condition characterized by agitation — it is called <s>bībhatsa</s> (the disgusting rasa). The <s>bhayānaka</s> (terrifying rasa) has frightening objects as its subject; its involuntary signs are drying of the mouth, licking of the palate, crouching low, and the like; its <s>sāttvika</s> reactions exclude tears; its transitory emotions are despondency, apprehension, terror, agitation, dejection, stupor, languor, fatigue, anxiety, epileptic seizure, and the like; and the permanent emotion of fear rests upon the very same plane characterized by agitation of the heart.
For example —

children.text: śrīsiṅgakṣitināyakasya ripavo dhāṭīśruterākulāḥ śuṣyattālupuṭaṃ skhalatpadatalaṃ vyālokayanto diśaḥ /
children.translated_text: The enemies of King <s>Siṅga</s>, the lord of the earth, thrown into confusion by hearing of his military expedition, with palates drying up, stumbling on their feet, looking in all directions,

children.text: dhāvitvā kathamapyupetya tamasā gāḍhopagūḍhāṃ guhām anviṣyanti tadantare 'pi karasaṃsparśena gartāntaram // Ckc_5.*23 //
children.translated_text: having somehow run and reached a cave tightly embraced by darkness, they search within it, even there, by the touch of their hands, for yet another cavity (to hide in). // Ckc_5.*23 //

children.text:
atra kriyākrūranāyakanāsīrabhaṭaviṣayaḥ śatrusamāśrayaḥ sthāyībhāvo dhāṭīśravaṇoddīpito dhāvanaguhāpraveśagartāntarānveṣaṇādibhi ranubhāvairabhivyakto vyākulatvatāluśoṣaṇa padaskhalanādyanumitairāvegaśaṅkātrāsādibhirvyabhicāribhirabhipuṣṭo bhāvakacetasi vikṣepalakṣaṇāṃ bhūmikāṃ bibhrāṇo bhayānaka ityākhyāyate /
seyamakhilo 'pi rasapuruṣārtho jananasāhasrasaṃpāditasāhityadevatāpadāravindayugalopāsanājanitavāsanāprauḍhaparipākabhāvanāviśeṣasahakāriṇāṃ sahṛdayānāṃ mānasena gocarī kṛto yena kenacidākāreṇa bhāsate /
nanu ko 'yamākāro rasasya yenāyaṃ bhāvakamānasairanubhūyata iti cetsvasvānubhavaikavedanīye tasminnākāre kathamasmādṛśāṃ vācovyāpāra mātmīyamāpūrayeyuḥ /
na hi kṣīrasāgaramāgalaṃ pibannapi taṃ mādhurīviśeṣamidaṃtayā nirdeṣṭuṃ brahmāpi śaknoti /
kintu vigalitavedyāntaratvamiti vacanaparipāṭīṃ manasi muhurāvartayatā bhāvanāsiddhiparyantaṃ saṃtoṣṭavyamāyuṣmatā /
children.translated_text: Here, the permanent emotion of fear, whose subject is the cruel hero's warrior <s>Nāsīrabhaṭa</s> and whose locus is the enemies, is enflamed by hearing of the military expedition, manifested by involuntary signs such as running, entering caves, and searching for cavities; nourished by transitory emotions such as agitation, apprehension, and terror inferred from confusion, drying of the palate, stumbling of feet, and the like — bearing in the connoisseur's heart the plane characterized by agitation — it is called <s>bhayānaka</s> (the terrifying rasa). This entire <s>rasa</s> — the ultimate purpose of human life (<s>puruṣārtha</s>) — shines forth in some form or other when experienced by the minds of the connoisseurs (<s>sahṛdaya</s>), whose matured disposition, produced by the worship of the lotus-feet of the goddess of literary art acquired through thousands of births, is accompanied by the special power of contemplation (<s>bhāvanā</s>) ripened to perfection. Now, what is this form of <s>rasa</s> by which it is experienced by the minds of connoisseurs? Since that form is knowable only through one's own individual experience, how could the verbal activity of people like us fulfill its own (capacity to describe) it? For even <s>Brahmā</s> himself, though drinking in the ocean of milk, cannot definitively point out that particular sweetness as 'this.' But one should be content — you who are long-lived — until the perfection of contemplation (<s>bhāvanāsiddhi</s>) is achieved, repeatedly turning over in one's mind the verbal tradition that says 'it is the dissolution of all other objects of knowledge.'
Now (an objection) —
By the maxim of 'castle in the sky,' this <s>rasa</s> is clearly (unreal);

children.text: āmīlitadṛśāṃ puṃsāṃ seyaṃ bhāvaka bhūmikā // Ckc_5.28 //
children.translated_text: this plane of the connoisseur is (merely the fancy) of men with half-closed eyes (i.e., dreamers). // Ckc_5.28 //
The establishment of the measurable depends on the measure — this is accepted by all schools of thought.

children.text: asatyo rasavādo 'yaṃ rasavāda itaḥ param // Ckc_5.29 //
children.translated_text: This doctrine of <s>rasa</s> is false; this 'doctrine of <s>rasa</s>' henceforth (is mere alchemy)! // Ckc_5.29 //
This (rasa) is not apprehensible by direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), nor is it established by inference (<s>anumāna</s>),

children.text: na cāgamena sugamo nopamānena mānitaḥ // Ckc_5.30 //
children.translated_text: nor is it easily accessible through scripture (<s>āgama</s>), nor established by analogy (<s>upamāna</s>). // Ckc_5.30 //

children.text:
samarthito nārthāpattyā nābhāvena ca ........ /
................ saṃbhāvyo naitihyena ca lihyate // Ckc_5.31 //
children.translated_text: It is not established by presumption (<s>arthāpatti</s>), nor by non-existence (<s>abhāva</s>)...

children.text:
iti ceducyate svānubhūtivilasanameva rasasya sadbhāve pramāmamiti paramaṃ rahasyam /
tadetadanupadameva pradarśitam /
anyā punariyaṃ vāgāḍaṃbaraviḍaṃbanā vividhacarcāvinodakaṃḍūladhiṣaṇāprakāṃḍānāṃ vādināṃ mude vilikhyate /
tathāhi /
nanu pratyakṣī bhavannasau nirvikalpakenāvabhāsate savikalpakena vā /
nādyaḥ /
vastusvarūpa mātrāvabhāsakasvabāvatvānnirvikalpakasya rasasya bhuvi bhāvadiviśeṣānusaṃdhānapūrvakapratītisvabhāvatvāt /
nirvikalpakapūrvatvātsavikalpakasyeti cet śrūyatām /
savikalpakeneti brūmaḥ /
savikalpakasya nirvikalpakapūrvakatvābhidhānamavijāritaramaṇīyameva /
nirviśiṣṭaviṣayānullekhino jñānasyaivāsaṃbhavāt /
tathā ca śeṣāvatāraviśeṣasya bhagavataḥ patañjalerabhiprāyaṃ prakaṭayatā vyāhṛtaṃ hariyoginā /
children.translated_text: If so, we reply: the supreme secret is that the shining forth of one's own experience (<s>svānubhūti</s>) itself is the valid means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) for the existence of <s>rasa</s>. This has already been demonstrated step by step. But this further verbal elaboration and refutation — this is written for the amusement of debaters whose intellects itch with the delight of various discussions. Thus: now, does this (rasa), when becoming directly perceptible, appear through non-conceptual cognition (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>) or through conceptual cognition (<s>savikalpaka</s>)? Not the first, because non-conceptual cognition by its nature only illuminates the mere essence of the object, while rasa, being of the nature of cognition preceded by the investigation of the particulars of the determinants (<s>vibhāva</s>) and the like on the earth (of experience), (cannot be non-conceptual). If one says that conceptual cognition must be preceded by non-conceptual — listen: we say it is through conceptual cognition. The statement that conceptual cognition must be preceded by non-conceptual is a charmingly unconsidered (assertion), since cognition that does not register a qualified object is simply impossible. And so, <s>Hariyogin</s>, revealing the intention of the blessed <s>Patañjali</s>, who is a special incarnation of <s>Śeṣa</s> (the serpent), has declared:
'There is no cognition in the world that is without the accompaniment of words.

children.text: anuviddhamiva jñānaṃ sarvaṃ śabdena gṛhyate // Ckc_5.32 //
children.translated_text: All knowledge is grasped as if pervaded by words.' // Ckc_5.32 //

children.text:
iti anumānamapi sāmānyato dṛṣṭam rasāvabhāsakatayātmani bahumānamākalyati /
amī sāmājikā rasānubhavavantaḥ /
ye ye vivakṣitaceṣṭāviśiṣṭāste te rasānubhavavantaḥ /
yathā tattvasākṣātkārānubhavitāraḥ /
tathā ceme ceṣṭāviśiṣṭāḥ /
tasmāt rasānubhavavanta eveti /
na ca dṛṣṭānte sādhanavaikalyamāśaṅkanīyam /
samādhivelāyāmānante bāṣpādivyatikaraprasiddheḥ /
children.translated_text: Inference too, of the commonly observed type, can claim authority as an illuminator of <s>rasa</s>. (The argument:) These members of the audience possess the experience of <s>rasa</s>. All who are characterized by the particular gestures that one wishes to speak of, possess the experience of <s>rasa</s> — just as those who experience the direct realization of truth (do). And these (audience members) are characterized by (such) gestures. Therefore they possess the experience of <s>rasa</s>. Nor should the deficiency of the evidence in the example be suspected, since at the time of meditative absorption (<s>samādhi</s>), the occurrence of tears and the like in the infinite (consciousness) is well established.
Thus in the <s>Mahimnaḥ Stava</s> (Hymn of Greatness) —

children.text: "manaḥ pratyak citte savidhamavadhāyāstamarutaḥ prahṛṣyadromāṇaḥ pramadasalilotsaṅgita dṛśaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Directing the mind inward to consciousness, restraining the breath, with hair standing on end from joy, with eyes brimming with tears of delight,

children.text: yadālokyāhlādahrada iva nimajjyāmṛtamaye dadhatyantastattvaṃ kamapi yaminastatkila bhavān" // Ckc_5.*24 //
children.translated_text: when, gazing (inward), they plunge as if into a lake of bliss, in that which is filled with nectar, those ascetics hold within themselves some ineffable truth — and that indeed is You.' // Ckc_5.*24 //
Thus.

children.text:
āgamāḥ puna ranekasiddhāntarahasye sākṣātkāriṇāṃ yathādṛṣṭavādināṃ purāṇakavīnāmalaṅkārasaṃhitāḥ /
tatra ca rasa eva sarvottaratayā pratipādyate /
gosadṛśo gavaya itivat tattvasākṣātkārasadṛśo rasa ityupamānamapi rasasadbhāvāyānubhāvanādātmasattāsāphalyamanusaṃdhatte /
arthāpattirapi nirāpattikaṃ samarthayate rasasadbhāvam /
yathā divā na bhuñjānasya devadattasya pīnatvānupapattyā kalpitā naktaṃbhuktiḥ /
evaṃ vibhāvānubhāvāderanupapattyā rasa iti /
nanu rasāpratītāvapi svayameva kvacidāsvādyatayā svatandrāṇāṃ bhāvādīnāṃ kānupapattiriti cet kadācit ko 'pi vibhāvādiṣu svatantravyavahāra upacāramātreṇa rājapuruṣeṣu rājavyavahāravaditi saṃbhavavastusaṃkhyāviṣayatayā rasamahārājalakṣmīmanālakṣayan nijadaurbhāgyamāvirbhāvayati /
aitihyamapi nidarśitapramāṇasaṃvādinā bāhyaṃ, naiva rasanirūpaṇe saṃbādhamavalambate /
taditthamakhilapramāṇasaṃsiddhe rasasudhāniṣyande sumanobhiranubhūyamāne yogyānupalabdhilakṣaṇamabhāvapramāṇaṃ rasāvamānaika durāgrahāṇāṃ viparītasākṣarāṇāṃ manasi vaidagdhyābhāvameko 'pi bhāsayati /
tathā coktamasmadācāryaiḥ kāśīśvaramiśraiḥ rasamīmāṃsāyām
children.translated_text: Scriptures (<s>āgama</s>), furthermore, are the literary treatises (<s>alaṅkārasaṃhitā</s>) of the ancient poets who, having directly realized (truth), spoke as they saw — (these are found) in the esoteric teachings of many schools. And therein, <s>rasa</s> alone is established as the supreme (purpose). Just as (one says) 'a <s>gavaya</s> (bison) is similar to a cow' — so too 'rasa is similar to the direct realization of truth' — analogy (<s>upamāna</s>) too, by bringing about the experience (of rasa), accomplishes the fruitfulness of its own existence for (proving) the reality of <s>rasa</s>. Presumption (<s>arthāpatti</s>) too establishes the reality of <s>rasa</s> without difficulty. Just as, for <s>Devadatta</s> who does not eat during the day, his corpulence being otherwise inexplicable, eating at night is postulated — so too, from the otherwise inexplicable (occurrence) of determinants, consequents, and the like, <s>rasa</s> (is postulated). If one objects that even without the apprehension of <s>rasa</s>, the emotions and the like, being independently relishable on their own somewhere, would have no inexplicability — then (we reply): the occasional independent operation among the determinants and the like is merely figurative, like the use of 'king' for king's men. One who, regarding such a matter that falls within the scope of enumeration, fails to perceive the sovereign majesty of <s>rasa</s>, merely reveals his own misfortune. Tradition (<s>aitihya</s>) too, being external and consonant with the demonstrated valid means, does not at all impede the determination of <s>rasa</s>. Thus, when <s>rasa</s> — this flow of nectar, established by all valid means of knowledge — is being experienced by the discerning, even the single valid means of qualified non-apprehension (<s>yogyānupalabdhi</s>) — the proof of absence — illuminates, in the minds of those who obstinately despise <s>rasa</s> (reading the letters perversely), the absence of aesthetic refinement. And so our teacher <s>Kāśīśvara Miśra</s> has said in the <s>Rasamīmāṃsā</s>:
'One who, disregarding the sovereign glory of <s>rasa</s>, (engages only in) the mere gateway of verbal grandiloquence,
is like sugarcane which, out of hatred of <s>rasa</s> (juice/aesthetic sentiment), experiences only the stiffness of its stalk.' // Ckc_5.33 //
The definitions of valid means of knowledge and the like are to be understood from elsewhere.
The poets, who operate with meanings established by worldly convention and philosophical conclusions,
are here indeed the sole witnesses of the direct realization of aesthetic wonder (<s>camatkāra</s>). // Ckc_5.34 //
The detailed characteristics and examples of others not mentioned here
(can be found) in the <s>Rasārṇavasudhākara</s> composed by King <s>Siṅgabhūpa</s>. // Ckc_5.35 //
They should be properly studied in the first and second chapters (thereof);
since our attention is fixed elsewhere, they have not been elaborated by us. // Ckc_5.36 //

children.text: na hi sarvatra sarveṣāṃ viśeṣāṇāṃ pradarśanam /
children.translated_text: For it is not (possible) to demonstrate all particulars everywhere;
there would be the fault of excessive prolixity, leading to the rupture of the treatise. // Ckc_5.37 //

children.text:
diṅmātrameva śāstreṣu dhīmatāmupadiśyate /
khayamevāvabhāsante viśeṣāḥ pariśīlanāt // Ckc_5.38 //
children.translated_text: In treatises, only a general indication is taught to the wise; the particulars manifest of themselves through (diligent) practice. // Ckc_5.38 //
Thus, all is auspicious.

children.text: iti sarasasāhityacāturīdhurīṇaviśveśvarakavicandrapraṇītāyāṃ śrīsiṅgabhūpālakīrtisudhāsāra śītalāyāṃ camatkāracandrikāyā- malaṅkṛtau rasaviveko nāma pañcamo vilāsaḥ //
children.translated_text: Thus ends the fifth <s>vilāsa</s> (chapter), named 'The Discrimination of <s>Rasa</s> in the domain of Ornament,' in the <s>Camatkāracandrikā</s>, composed by <s>Viśveśvara Kavicandra</s>, endowed with the skill of elegant literary art, cooled by the nectar-essence of the fame of King <s>Siṅgabhūpa</s>.
Sixth <s>Vilāsa</s> (Chapter).
The <s>Camatkāracandrikā</s>, composed by <s>Viśveśvara Kavicandra</s> — The <s>Alaṅkāra</s> (Figures of Speech) Chapter.
Those which, situated in a particular part (of the poem), adorn the entire body of the poem, like bracelets and the like (adorn the body),

children.text: alaṅkurvanti ye kāvyaṃ te 'laṅkāratayā matāḥ // Ckc_6.1 //
children.translated_text: are considered to be <s>alaṅkāra</s>s (figures of speech). // Ckc_6.1 //
Their threefold (classification) is stated, arising from word, meaning, and both.
Of these, eleven word-based (figures) are enumerated by the wise: // Ckc_6.2 //
<s>Chāyā</s> (imitation), <s>Mudrā</s> (seal/stamp), <s>Yukti</s> (device), <s>Śleṣa</s> (paronomasia), <s>Anuprāsa</s> (alliteration), <s>Gumbhana</s> (weaving), <s>Citra</s> (pictorial),

children.text: yamakaṃ vākovākyaṃ gūḍhaṃ praśnottaraṃ ceti // Ckc_6.3 //
children.translated_text: <s>Yamaka</s> (repetition), <s>Vākovākya</s> (dialogue), <s>Gūḍha</s> (concealed), and <s>Praśnottara</s> (question-and-answer). // Ckc_6.3 //

children.text:
anyoktīnāmanukṛtiḥ chāyā seyamudāhṛtā /
tredhā nāgarikagrāmyasāmānyoktyanusārataḥ // Ckc_6.4 //
children.translated_text: The imitation (<s>anukṛti</s>) of others' speech is <s>Chāyā</s> — it is illustrated (as being) of three kinds: based on urbane speech (<s>nāgarika</s>), rustic speech (<s>grāmya</s>), and common speech (<s>sāmānya</s>). // Ckc_6.4 //
An example of <s>Chāyā</s> of urbane speech —
He who, though sprinkled with the nectar-juice of the auspicious words of King <s>Siṅgabhūpa</s>,

children.text: yo na pallavitastasmai jaṅgamasthāṇave namaḥ // Ckc_6.*1 //
children.translated_text: has not sprouted (into bloom) — to that mobile tree-trunk, salutations! // Ckc_6.*1 //

children.text: atra jaṅgamasthāṇave nama iti solluṇṭhane namaḥśabdaṃ vadatāṃ vidagdhānāmukteranukṛtiḥ chāyā /
children.translated_text: Here, 'salutations to the mobile tree-trunk' — this is <s>Chāyā</s>, the imitation of the speech of the refined (<s>vidagdha</s>) who use the word '<s>namaḥ</s>' (salutation) in a mocking sense.
An example of <s>Chāyā</s> of rustic speech —
O friend, behold the royal elephants who have taken refuge at the pair of feet of King <s>Siṅga</s>.

children.text: sundari kimidaṃ citraṃ rājñi bhujaṅge 'pi kācavalayaḥ kim // Ckc_6.*2 //
children.translated_text: O beautiful one, what wonder is this? When it comes to a king (or a serpent), what (need) is there of a glass bangle? // Ckc_6.*2 //

children.text: atra turīyapāda āśrayaviśeṣeṇābyudayaviśeṣaṃ vadatāṃ grāmyāṇāmukteranukṛtiḥ chāyā /
children.translated_text: Here, in the fourth line, stating that through a special patron (<s>āśraya</s>), there is special prosperity — this is <s>Chāyā</s>, the imitation of the speech of the rustic.
An example of <s>Chāyā</s> of common speech —

children.text: ko 'yaṃ vāñchitamarthināṃ vitanute nanveṣa cintāmaṇiḥ sagrāvā kila kintu naiva hi pumān hāsena kiṃ bhūyasā /
children.translated_text: Who is this one who fulfills the desires of supplicants? 'He is a wish-fulfilling gem (<s>Cintāmaṇi</s>).' But he is (also) a stone! 'However, he is certainly not a man (either).' What need of more laughter?

children.text: so 'yaṃ śrī anavotasiṅganṛpatiḥ kasmādidaṃ jñāyate ratnollāsini kaṅbtṇe karatale kiṃ darpaṇāpekṣayā // Ckc_6.*3 //
children.translated_text: He is the glorious King <s>Anavota Siṅga</s>. How is this known? When a jewel shines on a bracelet on the hand, what need is there of a mirror? // Ckc_6.*3 //

children.text: atra turīyapāde pratyakṣasiddhe vastuni kimanyāpekṣayetyasminnarthe karakaṅkaṇadarśane kimādarśavimbeneti sarvajanasādhāraṇokteranukaraṇādiyaṃ sāmānyokticchāyā /
children.translated_text: Here, in the fourth line, regarding a matter established by direct evidence — 'what need of other (proof)?' — in this meaning, 'when looking at a bracelet on the hand, what need of a mirror?' — since it imitates common people's speech, this is <s>Chāyā</s> of common speech.
The embedding of a word with a particular intention within a sentence

children.text: mudrāṃ tāṃ mutpradāyitvāt kāvyamudrāvido viduḥ // Ckc_6.5 //
children.translated_text: is known by those versed in poetic <s>Mudrā</s> (seal) as that (figure called) <s>Mudrā</s>, because it produces wonder (<s>mut</s>). // Ckc_6.5 //

children.text: seyaṃ dvedhā budhairuktā padena vacanena ca // Ckc_6.6 //
children.translated_text: It is said by the learned to be of two kinds: through a word (<s>pada</s>) and through a sentence (<s>vacana</s>). // Ckc_6.6 //
An example of word-<s>Mudrā</s> (<s>padamudrā</s>) —

He devours the leaves of our wish-fulfilling creeper — let your desire-cow restrain (him); let my wish-fulfilling gem pedestals be transformed — keep the elephant of arrogance far from here at a great height.

children.text: ityārūḍhavitardikāḥ pratipadaṃ jalpanti bhūdevatāḥ siṅgakṣmābhuji kalpavṛkṣasurabhīhastyādidānodyate // Ckc_6.*4 //
children.translated_text: thus, having ascended the platforms, the gods of the earth (<s>Brāhmaṇas</s>) exclaim at every step, when <s>Siṅgakṣmābhuj</s> (King <s>Siṅga</s>) is engaged in the distribution of wish-tree[-like gifts], wish-fulfilling cows, elephants, etc. // Ckc_6.*4 //

children.text: atra kalpalatādīnāṃ devatāyogyatvāt sadbrāhnaṇā ityādipadato 'pi bhūdevatā iti padasyābhijātatvamitīyaṃ padamudrā /
children.translated_text: Here, since wish-granting vines etc. are appropriate only for deities, and from words like 'true <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>' also, the word '<s>bhūdevatā</s>' (gods of the earth) is more refined [than simply 'Brāhmaṇas'] — this is <s>padamudrā</s> (word-seal).
<s>Vacanamudrā</s> (sentence-seal) is as follows:

"O you who dwell in the precincts of the <s>cintāmaṇi</s> (wish-gem) platform, in the shade of the celestial wish-fulfilling trees, nourished by the streams of milk from the wish-fulfilling cow's udders —

children.text: mā garvīyata devatā vayamamī dṛṣṭāḥsma āvismitaiḥ śrīsiṅgakṣitināyakasya karuṇāraṅgairapāṅgaiḥ sphuṭam // Ckc_6.*5 //
children.translated_text: do not be proud, O deities! We have been clearly seen with wonder-struck [eyes] by the compassionate, playful sidelong glances of <s>Śrīsiṅgakṣitināyaka</s> (King <s>Siṅga</s>)." // Ckc_6.*5 //

children.text: atra devatāsāmyabahuvacanābhiprāyaṇātmani vaktrā vayamiti bahuvacanaṃ prayuktamitīyaṃ vacanamudrā /
children.translated_text: Here, in the intention of using the plural to convey equality with the deities, the speaker uses the plural 'we' — this is <s>vacanamudrā</s> (sentence-seal).
<s>Yukti</s> (contrivance) is the joining together of words being combined,

children.text: yojanā kriyate yāsau yuktirityucyate budhaiḥ // Ckc_6.7 //
children.translated_text: in a manner appropriate to the subject; that which is done — this is called <s>yukti</s> by the wise. // Ckc_6.7 //
There, the joining of [seemingly] unfit words is as follows:
Abiding in <s>Śambhu's</s> (<s>Śiva's</s>) ornament-casket, rivaling the co-wife of <s>Śrī</s> (<s>Lakṣmī</s>), shining forth on all sides,

children.text: viṣṇoḥ padaṃ madhyamamāviśantī virājate siṅganṛpālakīrtiḥ // Ckc_6.*6 //
children.translated_text: entering the middle abode of <s>Viṣṇu</s> — the fame of King <s>Siṅganṛpāla</s> is resplendent. // Ckc_6.*6 //

children.text:
atra pātālamityādi prakṛtārthe śambhubhūṣaṇapeṭikādi padānāmakleśayogaparaṃparayā yojanā kṛteti padayuktiriyam /
evaṃ vākyaprakaraṇaprabandhaviśeṣāṇāmapyudāhāraṇāni draṣṭavyāni /
children.translated_text: Here, in the primary meaning of 'the netherworld' etc., the words '<s>Śambhu's</s> ornament-casket' etc. are joined through a sequence of effortless connection — thus this is <s>padayukti</s> (word-contrivance). Likewise, examples of sentence-, section-, and composition-level [contrivance] should be observed.
<s>Śleṣa</s> (double entendre) is the expression of two meanings

children.text: tantreṇa yatra hi śleṣaḥ so 'yaṃ naikavidho mataḥ // Ckc_6.8 //
children.translated_text: through a single sentence by means of a pivot (<s>tantra</s>); it is considered of many kinds. // Ckc_6.8 //
Through stem, suffix, word, case-ending, number, etc. // Ckc_6.9 //
There, <s>prakṛtiśleṣa</s> (stem-level double entendre) is as follows:
"This servant of yours, <s>Kalyāṇada</s> (giver of auspiciousness), bows, O <s>Śrīsiṅgabhūpate</s>,
among those in the world who know the essence of wealth — among the learned and even among the enemies." // Ckc_6.*7 //

children.text: atra kalyāṇada ityatra dadātidadatyoḥ sāravidāmityatra vettividantyośca prakṛtyoḥ śleṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, in '<s>kalyāṇada</s>' there is a <s>śleṣa</s> of the two stems <s>dadāti</s> (gives) and <s>dadati</s> (they give); in '<s>sāravid</s>' of the two stems <s>vetti</s> (knows) and <s>vidanti</s> (they find) — this is stem-level <s>śleṣa</s>.
"O <s>Siṅgabhūpāla</s>, your hand brings joy to the learned;

children.text: kartā vairivipattīnāṃ saṃpadaṃ suhṛdāṃ sphuṭam // Ckc_6.*8 //
children.translated_text: the doer of the enemies' misfortunes, and clearly [the doer] of the prosperity of friends." // Ckc_6.*8 //

children.text:
tatra karteti pade tṛcpratyayatṛnpratyayayoḥ śleṣaḥ /
vairivipattīnāṃ karteti tṛcpratyayaḥ /
saṃpadaṃkarteti tṛnpratyayaḥ /
anyathā kṛdyogaṣaṣṭhyāvaśyaṃbhāvitvāttadubhayavibhaktisaṃbaṃdhāya pratyayadvayasya vivakṣitatvāt tathokto 'yam /
children.translated_text: Here, in the word '<s>kartā</s>' there is a <s>śleṣa</s> of the two suffixes <s>tṛc</s> and <s>tṛn</s>. '<s>Kartā</s>' with the <s>tṛc</s> suffix means 'the doer of enemies' misfortunes'; '<s>kartā</s>' with the <s>tṛn</s> suffix means 'the doer of [friends'] prosperity.' Otherwise, since the genitive must necessarily accompany a <s>kṛt</s>-derivative, the two suffixes are intended to serve the relation with both case-endings — thus it is so stated.
<s>Padaśleṣa</s> (word-level double entendre) is as follows:

children.text: hariścandro rakṣākaraṇarucisatyeṣu vacasāṃ vilāse vāgīśo mahati niyame nītinigame /
children.translated_text: <s>Hariścandra</s> in the delight of words whose truth is the beauty of conferring protection; <s>Vāgīśa</s> (Lord of Speech) in great restraint and the science of statecraft;

children.text: vijetā gāṅgeyaṃ janabharaṇa saṃmohanakalā- vrateṣu śrīsiṅgakṣitipatirudāro vijayate // Ckc_6.*9 //
children.translated_text: the conqueror — [like] <s>Gāṅgeya</s> (<s>Bhīṣma</s>), in the vows of deluding the people through sustenance — <s>Śrīsiṅgakṣitipati</s>, the generous one, triumphs! // Ckc_6.*9 //

children.text:
atra hariścandra iti cakravartivācake pade hariścandraścandraśceti padayoḥ vāgīśaḥ vāgīśaśceti padayoḥ gāṅgeya iti bhīṣma iti vācake pade gāṅgoyaṃ ceti padayoḥ śleṣaḥ, ityayaṃ padaśleṣaḥ /
vibhaktiśleṣo dvidhā /
sajātīyo vijātīya iti /
children.translated_text: Here, in '<s>Hariścandra</s>' — a word denoting a universal sovereign — the two words '<s>Hariś</s>' and '<s>candraś ca</s>' have a <s>śleṣa</s>; in '<s>Vāgīśa</s>' the two words '<s>Vāgīśaḥ</s>' [the deity] and '<s>vāg-īśaḥ</s>' [lord of speech]; in '<s>Gāṅgeya</s>' — a word denoting <s>Bhīṣma</s> — the two words '<s>gāṅgaḥ ayam</s>' [this one of the Ganges]. This is word-level <s>śleṣa</s>. <s>Vibhaktiśleṣa</s> (case-ending double entendre) is of two kinds: <s>sajātīya</s> (same-class) and <s>vijātīya</s> (different-class).
The first is as follows:
"Bearing on his chest the king of birds (<s>virāj</s>) residing in the lotus, and the <s>Kaustubha</s> gem —
may the Lord (<s>Deva</s>) protect <s>Śrīsiṅgabhūpati</s>!" // Ckc_6.*10 //

children.text:
atra vīnāṃ pakṣiṇāṃ rāṭ tasmin virājīti saptamī /
lakṣmīkaustubhābhyāṃ virājī virājanaśīlamiti dvitīyā /
tedve subvibhakttī virājīti pade śliṣṭeiti sajātīyavibhaktiśleṣo 'yam /
children.translated_text: Here, '<s>virāj</s>' meaning 'king of birds [dwelling] in it' takes the locative case; and '<s>virāj</s>' meaning 'shining through <s>Lakṣmī</s> and the <s>Kaustubha</s>' takes the instrumental case. These two sub-case-endings are conflated in the word '<s>virāji</s>' — this is <s>sajātīya vibhaktiśleṣa</s> (same-class case-ending double entendre).
The second is as follows:

children.text: kīrtirviśālā dviṣatāmahāri vyatāni tadvāmadṛśāṃ ca vakṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: "The fame [of the enemies] was vast — carried away by <s>Śrīsiṅgabhūpa</s>; the chests of their beautiful-eyed women were spread open;

children.text: abhedi taddurgamapi vyadhāyi śrīsiṅgabhūpena nijāptacittam // Ckc_6.*11 //
children.translated_text: their fortresses too were split; and the hearts of his own people were established [in trust]." // Ckc_6.*11 //

children.text:
atra nāyakena dviṣatāṃ kīrtirahāri hṛtā /
tenaiva ripustrīṇāṃ vakṣaḥ avidyamānahāraṃ vyatānītyatra atītyekapade luṅi prathamapuruṣaśca napuṃsakakarma ca dvitīyā ca tiṅsubvibhakttī śliṣṭe iti vijātīyavibhaktiśleṣaḥ /
evamabhedītyatrāpi vijñeyam /
children.translated_text: Here, the fame of the enemies was '<s>ahāri</s>' (carried away); and the chests of the enemy women '<s>avyatāni</s>' (without necklaces / spread open) — in this, the word '<s>atīt</s>' in the past tense has conflated the third person and neuter object with the second person, making the verbal and nominal case-endings conflate — this is <s>vijātīya vibhaktiśleṣa</s> (different-class case-ending double entendre). Likewise, in '<s>abhedi</s>' it should be understood [similarly].
<s>Vacanaśleṣa</s> (number-level double entendre) is as follows:
"The source of wishes, the boundary of prosperities, with an arm that protects the good, auspicious,
<s>Śauri</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>) and the gods — may they bestow auspiciousness upon <s>Siṅgabhūbhuj</s> (King <s>Siṅga</s>)." // Ckc_6.*12 //

children.text:
atra śauriḥ nārāyaṇo nāyakāya kalyāṇaṃ dadatāṃ vitaratu /
dada dāne iti dhātorātmanepadino loṭi prathamapuruṣaivakacanam /
kīdṛśaḥ śauriḥ /
āśānāṃ natajanamanorathānāṃ prabhava utpattisthānaṃ dātetyarthathaḥ śriyāṃ saubhāgyaviṣye sīmā paramāvadhiḥ /
satastrāyata iti sattraḥ /
tādṛśo bhujo bāhurasyeti sattrabhujaḥ /
śobhanā bhāso dīptayo 'syeti śubhāḥ devapakṣe tu devāḥ /
kalyāṇaṃ dadatāṃ vitarantu /
dadatāmiti ḍudāñ dāne iti dhātorātmanepadino loṭi prathamapuruṣabahuvacanam /
kiṃ bhūtāḥ devāḥ? āśānāṃ diśāṃ prabhavo nāthāḥ, śriyāṃ saṃpadāṃ sīmā avadhayaḥ /
satre bhujata iti satrabhujaḥ /
śobhanā bhāḥ kāntiḥ yeṣāṃ te śubā ityuktamārgeṇa kriyāpade viśeṣaṇapataṃ ekavacanabahuvacane śliṣṭe ityayaṃ vacanaśleṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, '<s>Śauri</s>' — <s>Nārāyaṇa</s> — may bestow auspiciousness upon the hero. '<s>Dadatām</s>' is the third-person singular imperative of '<s>dada</s>' (to give) in <s>ātmanepada</s>. What kind of <s>Śauri</s>? He is the source of wishes (the desires of his suppliants), the supreme limit of beauties. '<s>Sattra-bhuja</s>' means 'one who protects the good.' '<s>Śubhā</s>' means 'having beautiful radiance.' In the deity interpretation: the gods — may they bestow auspiciousness! '<s>Dadatām</s>' here is the third-person plural imperative of '<s>ḍudāñ</s>' (to give) in <s>ātmanepada</s>. What kind of gods? Lords of the directions, boundaries of prosperities; '<s>sattra-bhuja</s>' means 'those who eat at sacrifices'; '<s>śubha</s>' means 'those having beautiful radiance.' Thus, by the method described, the singular and plural numbers are conflated in the verb form — this is <s>vacanaśleṣa</s> (number-level double entendre).
From the word '<s>ādi</s>' (etc.), <s>bhāṣāśleṣa</s> (language-level double entendre) is as follows:
"May kingship be yours for [the purpose of] assemblage, O <s>Gādana Siṅgana</s>!
O valiant one, O banner of the citizens' delight, the <s>Ketana</s> of the city-women's <s>Rāma</s>!" // Ckc_6.*13 //

children.text:
he gādana ! gadayati pūrvamabhibhāṣayatīti gādanaḥ /
tasya saṃbuddhiḥ pūrvabhibhāṣinnityarthaḥ /
tādṛśāya te rājyam /
paurarāmākāṭanaketana paurarāmāṇāṃ porastrīṇāṃ kāṭanaketana matsyaketana rāmāmadanetyarthaḥ /
he sigana siṅgabhūpāla /
manasā vīrāya melāyanāya /
mā ca ilā ca mete lakṣmībhūmyau tayorayanaṃ mārgaḥ melāyanaṃ tasmai melāyanāya lakṣmībhūminivāsasthānāyetyarthaḥ /
tādṛśāya te rājyamiti prajāpālanasāmarthyarūpakarmāstu sarvotkarṣeṇa bhūyāditi saṃskṛtabhāṣā pratīyate /
melāyanāyetyādipadeṣu bhadramabhavadve tyādyārthavāciṣu taddeśabhāṣāviduṣāmāndhrabhāṣā ca pratīyate /
tadayaṃ bhāṣāśleṣaḥ /
evaṃ saṃskṛtaprākṛtādibhāṣāśleṣāstu tatra tatra mahākaviprabandheṣu citratareṣu svayamanusaṃdheyāḥ /
children.translated_text: O <s>Gādana</s>! — meaning 'one who speaks first, who greets first.' The vocative of that. 'Kingship be yours, O such one.' '<s>Paurarāmākāṭanaketana</s>' means 'the love-banner of the city women, the maddener of beautiful women.' O <s>Siṅgana</s>, O <s>Siṅgabhūpāla</s>! 'For the valiant one, for <s>Melāyana</s>' — <s>mā</s> and <s>ilā</s> mean <s>Lakṣmī</s> and Earth; their path (<s>ayana</s>) is <s>melāyana</s>, meaning 'the abode of <s>Lakṣmī</s> and Earth.' 'May such a kingship, in the form of the capacity to protect subjects, be yours in all its supremacy' — thus the Sanskrit meaning is understood. In the same words '<s>Melāyanāya</s>' etc., which in the regional language convey the meaning of 'auspiciousness be upon you' etc. — for those learned in that regional language, the <s>Āndhra</s> (Telugu) meaning is also perceived. This is <s>bhāṣāśleṣa</s> (language-level double entendre). Likewise, double entendres between Sanskrit and Prakrit and other languages should be investigated by the reader in the marvelous compositions of great poets.
<s>Anuprāsa</s> (alliteration) is the repetition of consonants in close proximity;
it is of two kinds in brief: <s>avyāpaka</s> (non-pervasive) and <s>vyāpaka</s> (pervasive). // Ckc_6.10 //
<s>Avyāpaka</s> (non-pervasive alliteration) is as follows:

children.text: gauḍīsaṅgītabhaṅgī rahasi vilasitaṃ kosalīkauśalānāṃ nepālīgaṇḍapālī mṛgamadamakarīṃ kairalīṃ pānakelīm /
children.translated_text: "The style of <s>Gauḍī</s> music, the secretly displayed skill of <s>Kosalī</s> [women], the <s>Nepālī</s> cheek-guard of musk-patterns, the <s>Kairalī</s> wine-sport,

children.text: lāṭīpāṭīracarcāṃ kusumaviracanāṃ kuntalīkuntalānāṃ siṅgakṣmākānta bhinte tava vijayaramāsnighdhaveṇiḥ kṛpāṇiḥ // Ckc_6.*14 //
children.translated_text: the <s>Lāṭī</s> sandalwood-paste application, the floral arrangement of <s>Kuntalī</s> tresses — O <s>Siṅgakṣmākānta</s>, your victory-<s>Lakṣmī's</s> affectionate braid, [your] sword, splits [them all]!" // Ckc_6.*14 //
Here, since the alliteration has different forms in each sentence-quarter, this is <s>avyāpaka anuprāsa</s> (non-pervasive alliteration).
And also:
"Victorious is the world-exalted one, far removed from base conduct, devoted to serving the good, favorable to praiseworthy truth,
the son of <s>Anavota</s>, a new celestial wish-cow, dense in qualities praised by the earth — the moon-like <s>Siṅgabhūpāla</s>." // Ckc_6.*15 //
Here, the alliteration at the beginning and end of words has different forms in each quarter.
<s>Vyāpaka anuprāsa</s> (pervasive alliteration) is as follows — in the hero's genealogy:
"Where [his enemies'] foot-army becomes grass-footed [destroyed], and there is departure from their own city,

children.text: vanacaraṇaṃ taccaraṇakaparicaraṇaṃ vā virodhināṃ śaraṇam // Ckc_6.*16 //
children.translated_text: forest-roaming, or attendance upon the feet of his servants — that is the refuge of the adversaries." // Ckc_6.*16 //

children.text:
atra rephaṇakārayugalasya sarvatrānuvṛttatvādyvāpakānuprāso 'yam /
evaṃ vṛttilāṭānuprāsātayo draṣṭavyāḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, since the pair of <s>repha</s> (r) and <s>ṇa</s> consonants recurs everywhere, this is <s>vyāpaka anuprāsa</s> (pervasive alliteration). Likewise, <s>vṛtti</s>- and <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s> should be observed.

children.text: śabdasya prakṛte samyagghaṭanā guṃphanā matā // Ckc_6.11 //
children.translated_text: <s>Gumphanā</s> (verbal weaving) is considered the proper fitting of a word into the subject. // Ckc_6.11 //
Here, 'word' is of two kinds: meaningless and borrowed (<s>anyagrathita</s>). Of the first:
For example:
"The enemies, newly occupied by the departure-drums of <s>Śrīsiṅgakṣitipāla's</s> battle-victory campaign resounding with praises,

children.text: svacchāyāmanudhāvinīṃ pratibhaṭānāśaṅkya śaṅkākulāstrāyadhvaṃ be be be iti pratipadaṃ jalpanti dhāvanti ca // Ckc_6.*17 //
children.translated_text: suspecting their own shadows running after them to be rival warriors, anxious, exclaiming 'be be be' at every step — they speak and run!" // Ckc_6.*17 //

children.text:
atra be ityādi nirarthakaśabdasya prastutānuguṇyena grathanādiyaṃ nirarthakaśabdaguṃphanā /
anyagrathitaśabdaguṃphanā trividhā /
pādaguṃphanā pādadvayaguṃphanā pādatrayaguṃphanāṃ ceti /
children.translated_text: Here, the meaningless sound '<s>be</s>' etc. is woven in conformity with the subject — this is <s>nirarthakaśabda-gumphanā</s> (weaving of meaningless words). Borrowed-word-weaving (<s>anyagrathita</s>) is of three kinds: quarter-verse weaving, half-verse weaving, and three-quarter-verse weaving.
The first is as follows:

children.text: arthasya puruṣo dāsa iti vakta vyalajjatām /
children.translated_text: "A person is the slave of wealth" — let the speaker of this be ashamed!

children.text: dāso hi puruṣasyārthaḥ paśyataḥ siṅgabhūpatim // Ckc_6.*18 //
children.translated_text: For indeed wealth is the slave of the person — just look at <s>Siṅgabhūpati</s>! // Ckc_6.*18 //
Here, since the previously quoted first [quarter-verse] is fitted in conformity with the subject, this is borrowed quarter-verse weaving.
The second is as follows:
"Youthful, with arms long from age-long exercise, broad-shouldered, door-chested, thick-necked" —

children.text: itīdamanyatra kavitvapaddhati- rvigāhate siṅganṛpe tu sārthatām // Ckc_6.*19 //
children.translated_text: this [expression] from elsewhere, a path of poetic composition, enters into truth only in the case of King <s>Siṅga</s>. // Ckc_6.*19 //
Here, since the first half, composed by <s>Kālidāsa</s>, is fitted in conformity with the subject, this is half-verse weaving.
The third is as follows:
"With form unsurpassed by those of the same class and those of different classes,
continuing as long as <s>rasa</s> endures" — [such] <s>Siṅgabhūpati</s> is resplendent! // Ckc_6.*20 //

children.text: atra pūrvālaṅkāraśāstrakāragra thitasyāpi pādatrayasya prathamārdhe sapakṣairvipakṣaiścānatikramaṇīyo yāvadrasaṃ vartamāna iti prastutānuguṇyena ghaṭanādiyaṃ pādatrayaguphanā /

children.translated_text: <s>Citra</s> (visual poetry), such as wheel-patterns and the like, is not approved by all poets;
because it obstructs the blossoming of <s>rasa</s> and is solely a cause of mental strain. // Ckc_6.12 //

Here, even though three quarters are borrowed from a previous <s>alaṅkāra</s>-treatise author, since the first half — '[unsurpassed] by allies and opponents, continuing as long as <s>rasa</s> endures' — is fitted in conformity with the subject [of praising the king], this is three-quarter-verse weaving.
<s>Cakrabandha</s> (wheel-pattern) is as follows:

children.text: sakṣamācakradiśāvilāsivibhunā tigmāṃśuhāriśriyā viśrāmakṣaṇaviśvaraṅgaviyatā kalpaṃ yaśo jyotiṣā /
children.translated_text: "By the fame like a luminary that is the repose-moment of the cosmic stage, with the splendor that steals the radiance of the fierce-rayed [sun], with the grace of [ruling] the wheel of regions,

children.text: vidvatkāntimavāpa yaḥ praviśadāvirbhūtakṛtsnāgamāṃ māṃdhātā sa ca tadviśeṣaviduṣo yāti tviṣā nopamām // Ckc_6.*21 //
children.translated_text: he attained the beauty dear to the learned, entering as the manifestation of all scriptures — that <s>Māṃdhātā</s>, knowing the distinction of that [fame], attains no comparison in brilliance." // Ckc_6.*21 //

children.text:
atra nemimārabhya tṛtīyasminnantare camatkārajyotsneti kṛtināma /
saptame viśvapatikaviriti tatkartṛnāma /
navame nāyakanāma ca prakaṭīkriyate /
ādiśabdātpaṅabandhādayaḥ /
